Testing a claim of love by whether someone walks behind you was an argument the audience already used on each other.
studies.didYouKnow: This is the only ayah in the Quran that states conditions for God loving a particular person. It makes that love a result of the person's own act. Elsewhere the text describes the kinds of people God loves: the just, the patient, those who keep clean. Here the relationship is put as an if and then, with the human move coming first.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes love checkable without making it mechanical. Following is offered as evidence, not as payment. So the divine response stays a gift while the human claim becomes testable. It also fixes the shape of religious life around a person rather than a system, which is a large claim about how God is approached. The closing names make sure that failing the test is not the end of the matter.

crossReferences.why: Describes a people God loves and who love Him, the same relationship stated from both sides.
Names the Messenger as a beautiful example for whoever hopes for God and the Last Day.
States that obeying the Messenger is obeying God, which is the logic behind this condition.

studies.applyIt: Pick one small practice you know came from the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and that you do not currently do. How he ate, how he greeted people, how he slept. Take one of them up this week for its own sake. This ayah makes love visible in ordinary movements rather than in strong feelings, and the smallest ones count.
studies.explainEasier: If you say you love God, then follow the way His messenger showed. Then God will love you back and forgive what you got wrong. God forgives, and He is kind.

studies.title: One Line, Chosen And Continued
studies.meaning: A short instruction is followed by a family line of chosen people. Four are named: the first human being, the survivor of the flood, and two families. Then a single phrase ties them together, describing them as offspring one from another. The classical scholars read that as real descent in part, and as a shared calling throughout, since Adam has no ancestors among them. The point of the list is continuity. It prepares the account of Mary and Jesus that follows.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The surah is establishing shared ground with communities who honour these same figures, and it does so by naming them in one sequence under one act of choosing. The family of Imran is introduced here for the first time, and the surah takes its name from that phrase. What follows immediately is a story of a birth, a dedication and a prophecy, all set inside this frame of selection.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to take the clear part of something, as one skims what is pure from a liquid. It implies selection for a purpose rather than preference, and the form stresses the act of choosing.
From a root associated with scattering, as seed is scattered. The word covers descendants across many generations, so it names a line stretching forward rather than a set of children.
A plural covering every category of created being, not humanity alone. Setting the chosen against that background makes the selection universal in scope rather than tribal or local.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Family line was the organising fact of Arabian life. A man's name carried his father and his grandfather. Trained reciters held the lines of whole tribes in memory. Inheritance, marriage, alliance and blood claims all ran along those lines. Presenting the prophets as a single descent spoke the audience's own language. It used the one frame everybody in the room already trusted.
studies.didYouKnow: Surah 3 takes its name from the phrase family of Imran, which occurs nowhere else in the Quran. Several surahs are named for a word that appears only once inside them. The name works as an identifier rather than a summary, which is how most Quranic surah names function.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Choosing is shown as continuous, not as a series of breaks. That shapes how the later prophets are read. Because the line is described as offspring one from another, no messenger arrives as a break with the one before him. The passage also puts all of them under a single act of choosing. That makes disagreements between the communities who honour them differences inside one story.

crossReferences.why: Lists prophets from the offspring of Adam, Noah, Abraham and Israel as one continuous line.
Traces the same descent across many names, saying each was guided and chosen.
Shows Abraham handing the same religion to his sons as a thing inherited.

studies.applyIt: Say the names in this ayah slowly. Notice how many belong to other people's traditions as much as to yours. That overlap is not an accident of history. The passage presents it as the design. Today, if the chance comes up, mention the shared line to someone of a different faith rather than the point where you part ways.
studies.explainEasier: God says to obey him and his Messenger. He chose Adam, Noah, the family of Abraham and the family of Imran above everyone else. They came one from another, a single line. God hears and knows.

studies.title: A Vow Made Before Birth
studies.meaning: A woman speaks before her child is born and gives that child away in advance. She dedicates what is in her womb to God's service. She attaches no condition and asks for nothing back. Her only request is that the offering be accepted. The classical scholars dwell on the word she uses, which means freed from other claims. They read it as releasing the child from the ordinary duties owed to a household. The woman herself is not named.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening the surah's account of the family the chapter is named for. The scene belongs to an earlier community, in a sanctuary kept by dedicated servants. The Quran gives no date and names no ruler. The classical commentaries add details from earlier traditions but treat them as extras. They hold to what the passage itself reports about the vow and the answer given to it.

keyTerms.note: The verb for binding oneself to give something to God. A vow in this vocabulary transfers ownership, so what is vowed leaves the giver's disposal from the moment the words are spoken.
A passive participle from the root for liberation. Commentators read it as freed from service to anyone but God, so the child is dedicated by being released rather than by being assigned.
An intensified form of the verb to receive. It asks not merely that the gift be taken but that it be received with favour, which is why the answer two ayat later repeats the same root.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A child in the ancient world was a labour force and an old-age pension. Sons worked, defended and inherited. Daughters married into alliances that held a household's place. Promising an unborn child to a sanctuary meant giving up the return on the biggest investment a family ever made. Anyone listening in seventh-century Arabia, where children counted as wealth, would have felt the size of it.
studies.didYouKnow: The woman who speaks these words is not named in the Quran, though the tradition preserves a name for her. The Quran names only one woman directly, Mary, who is the child being dedicated here. Everyone else, including this mother, is identified by relationship, which makes the naming of her daughter a few ayat later stand out.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows a gift offered before its value is known. Neither the child's sex nor its future is available to the one making the vow. That makes it an act of trust, not a trade. It also shows a woman's private words entering scripture as the opening of a prophetic history. The start of this line sits in a room nobody witnessed, not in a public event.

crossReferences.why: Continues the scene: the child is born a daughter, and the mother responds in prayer.
Shows Abraham settling his family near the Sacred House with a prayer of dedication.
Presents another parent offering a child, and a son who consents to the offering.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are protecting because you expect a return from it later: a child's path, a career move, a friendship you are quietly managing. Try saying, privately, that the outcome is not yours to hold. Say it once and change nothing. Then notice how much of your planning had assumed you held the deciding vote.
studies.explainEasier: Imran's wife prayed to God before her baby was born. She promised the child to him, set apart for his service. She asked God to take her gift, and said that he hears and knows.

studies.title: I Have Delivered A Female
studies.meaning: The vow assumed a son, since dedicated service in that sanctuary was men's work, and the child is a girl. The mother reports this to God almost as an apology. Then a clause interrupts her: God knew better what she had delivered. Scholars differ over whether the line about the male not being like the female continues her speech or comes as a comment on it, and the two readings pull opposite ways, one conceding a shortfall and one denying it. She names the child and asks protection for her and her descendants.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, carrying on the account of the family of Imran that opens the surah's central story. The passage speaks into a world where a daughter was widely felt to be a lesser outcome. The Quran addresses that attitude directly elsewhere. The classical commentaries note that the vow had been framed for a son. They note that the answer given went beyond what was asked. That is the point the next ayah develops.

keyTerms.note: The everyday verb for setting something down, used of giving birth. The plainness matters: the mother reports the fact without ornament, and the pronoun already carries the disappointment she is naming.
A comparative from the root for knowledge, dropped in as an aside in the middle of her speech. It corrects the assumption behind her report without addressing her directly or rebuking her.
A passive participle from the root meaning to stone or pelt. It names the adversary by what has been done to him, expelled and pursued, rather than by any power he is imagined to hold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In much of seventh-century Arabia the birth of a daughter was met with silence. The Quran elsewhere describes a father hiding from his people at the news. He weighs whether to keep the child in shame or bury her. Daughters made bride talks harder, could not raid, and left the household at marriage. A mother saying she had delivered a girl was reporting into that air.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman called by name in the Quran, and this is where her name first appears. She is named thirty-four times, more often than she is named in the Gospels, and a whole surah carries her name. The naming happens here inside her mother's own speech rather than in the narrative voice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's acceptance is shown not matching the terms of the offer. A vow was made in one shape and answered in another. The answer turns out to be the larger of the two. The aside about God knowing better also settles something. The worth of a person is not fixed by the categories a culture puts on them. That is the ground the whole story that follows rests on.

crossReferences.why: Gives the answer to this prayer: a gracious acceptance, and a growth described as beautiful.
Describes how a daughter's birth was received in that society, and judges the reaction.
Names Mary again as one who confirmed the words of her Lord and was among the devout.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you got an outcome you had not asked for and quietly filed as second best. Give it another look now, with the distance you have gained. The aside in this ayah is short and easy to miss: God knew better what was delivered. See whether anything on your own list has since turned out to be the larger answer.
studies.explainEasier: When the baby was born, the mother said she had given birth to a girl. God knew exactly what she had borne. She named the child Mary, and asked God to keep her and her children safe.

studies.title: Provision Without Reckoning
studies.meaning: Three verbs describe the answer to the mother's prayer: God received the child graciously, made her grow well, and placed her in a guardian's care. The word for growth is one normally used of plants. The scene then narrows to a repeated event. Her guardian keeps finding food with her that he did not bring, and her answer names the source without explaining the mechanism. The closing clause widens it out: God provides beyond calculation, to whom He wills.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's account of the family of Imran. The passage brings in Zechariah as Mary's guardian. That sets up his own prayer for a child in the ayat right after. Early scholars discuss what the provision was and differ over the details. Several report fruit out of its season. They agree the weight of the scene falls on what the guardian sees, not on what he is told.

keyTerms.note: A verb used of God bringing plants up out of the earth. Applying it to a child's upbringing borrows the imagery of cultivation: growth tended from outside and unfolding of its own accord.
A word for the innermost part of a place of prayer, and elsewhere for a raised or private room. It marks a space set apart, one that is entered deliberately rather than passed through.
Literally without an account being kept. The phrase can mean without measure and also without the recipient being held to account for it, and the commentators keep both senses open.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Food came in seasons and everybody knew which. Dates arrived in late summer, grain after the rains. What you ate in a given month was steady enough to be everyday talk. Storage was small and costly. Finding fruit out of its season was no small wonder in that world. It broke a calendar that everyone planned their year around.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the sanctuary chamber occurs only a handful of times in the Quran. Two of those are in this surah, in the account of Mary and Zechariah. Another belongs to the same episode retold in a later surah. It went on to become the ordinary Arabic word for the niche in a mosque wall that marks the direction of prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers the mother's worry about her daughter without ever taking it up. It does not argue that a girl can serve. It shows the child receiving what nobody arranged for her. Provision is shown as loose from the visible channels that usually carry it. That does not make those channels unreal. It only takes them out of the place of final cause. The closing clause carries this far beyond the story.

crossReferences.why: Promises provision from where one does not expect it, for whoever is mindful of God.
Shows Mary provided for again, alone beneath a palm tree, at the birth of her son.
States that provision is in the heaven, together with what is being promised.

studies.applyIt: Look back over the past year for something that arrived without your arranging it: an introduction, a piece of timing, help from someone you barely knew. Name one. Then resist explaining how it came about. The guardian in this scene asks where it came from and gets no mechanism in reply, only a source, and he accepts that as an answer.
studies.explainEasier: God took Mary in and helped her grow up well. Zechariah looked after her. Every time he came in, he found food with her. She said it came from God, who gives to whoever he wants.

studies.title: The Prayer Of An Old Man
studies.meaning: The word that opens the ayah means at that point, and it ties the prayer to what Zechariah has just seen: provision arriving for Mary from a source he cannot account for. Watching one unexplained gift, he asks for another. The request is for good offspring, and the reason given for asking is not his need but God's nature, that He hears prayer. Early scholars note that the prayer follows evidence rather than despair.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. This sits in its account of the family of Imran, which runs from Mary's mother's vow through Mary's upbringing to the birth of John and then of Jesus. Zechariah is her guardian in the sanctuary. The passage does not date the events. Early scholars fill the story out from the wider tradition, while noting how compressed the Quran's own telling is.

keyTerms.note: A demonstrative of place that early scholars read here as also of time. It links the prayer directly to the moment before it, so the request is a response to something just witnessed.
The adjective means wholesome, clean and pleasant, used of food and of soil. He asks not for a child but for a particular quality of child, and early scholars highlight that precision.
A construction that makes hearing prayer a defining description rather than an occasional act. He states the ground of his request as an attribute of God rather than as anything about himself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Childlessness in a society built on family lines was a specific, public grief. A man without sons had nobody to carry his name into the family records that shaped every claim. Nobody would inherit his trade. In old age he had no protection beyond the goodwill of nephews. An audience hearing an old man ask for a child would have heard a request about carrying on, and about safety, as much as about love.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran tells the story of Zechariah's prayer three times: here, in surah nineteen, and in surah twenty-one. Each telling brings out something different. Here it is the sanctuary and Mary. In surah nineteen it is the whisper and the frailty of his bones. Surah twenty-one gives the shortest version of all. Early scholars treat the three as filling each other out, not as repeating.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer is prompted by a sign. That suggests seeing God act for someone else is grounds for asking on your own behalf, rather than for envy. Zechariah also asks for something the body says is unlikely, and the ayat around this show him surprised when it is granted. The Quran records that without criticism. Honest astonishment at an answered prayer is left standing as part of what faith looks like.

crossReferences.why: Retells the same prayer with the detail of his whispered call and his fear for his successors.
Gives the shortest version and adds that he called on God in hope and in awe.
Describes the provision found with Mary, the sign that prompts this prayer.

studies.applyIt: The next time you notice something going unexpectedly well for someone else, use it as Zechariah did. Treat it as evidence. Then let it prompt you to ask for your own long-abandoned request. Most people meet another's good news with comparison. Try meeting one instance of it this week with a prayer of your own instead, said at once, while the impression is fresh.
studies.explainEasier: Zechariah was old and had no children. He saw God give food to Mary out of nowhere. So he asked God for a good child of his own, because God hears people who ask.

studies.title: Called While Standing In Prayer
studies.meaning: The answer to a long prayer arrives during the prayer itself, not afterwards. Angels call out while the man is still standing. The promised son is described in four terms. He will confirm a word from God. He will be a leader. He will be restrained. And he will be a prophet among the upright. The classical scholars differ over the third. Some read it as self-restraint in general. Others read it as a life lived without marriage.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, carrying on the account of the family of Imran. It moves from Mary's upbringing to her guardian's own request. The scene belongs to an earlier community, in a sanctuary kept by dedicated servants. The guardian was old and had no children. The classical sources retell the episode more fully from earlier traditions, while keeping the Quran's order. That order puts his request straight after what he had been seeing.

keyTerms.note: Understood by the commentators as referring to Jesus, whom this surah names with the same term a few ayat later. An abstract noun is used for a person, which is the passage's own way of introducing him.
From a root meaning to precede or to take charge. It describes someone others defer to for his qualities rather than for any office, and here it is applied to a child not yet born.
An intensive form from a root meaning to confine or to besiege. Commentators differ over whether it names control of desire in general or a life without marriage, and the word carries both.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Having no children in the ancient Near East was a social state as much as a private grief. Property passed to side branches of the family. A man's name ended with him. Nobody was left to press the family's claims. An old man with no son had already begun to fade out of his own community's arrangements. What is announced here turns around a standing, not just a disappointment.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah places two birth announcements within a few ayat of each other. One goes to a man in old age. One goes to a young woman. Angels deliver both, in closely similar wording. In each case the person asks how such a thing can happen. And in each case the answer comes back in the same form.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The scene shows that an answer can arrive inside the act of asking. That changes the relation between a prayer and its result. It also brings in Jesus sideways, as a word to be confirmed, before he is named at all. That order serves the surah's argument. The one who will testify to him is announced first. So his coming reads as expected, not as a break in the story.

crossReferences.why: Retells the same episode at greater length, including the prayer that preceded this announcement.
Announces the other birth in the same terms, and names the word from God directly.
Recalls the same request and answer, adding that the household was quick in good works.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether you finish your requests to God and then leave the room, mentally, to go and wait. In this scene the answer arrives while the man is still standing. The next time you ask for something that matters, stay a moment longer than feels natural before you get up and start arranging it yourself.
studies.explainEasier: While he was standing and praying, angels called out to him. They said God was giving him good news of a son called John. John would confirm a word from God. He would be a leader, and good, and a prophet.

studies.title: How Will I Have A Son
studies.meaning: The man who has just received exactly what he asked for responds with a question about mechanism. He is old, his wife cannot bear children, and he says both things plainly. The reply does not address the obstacle at all. It repeats a single word meaning even so, then states that God does whatever He wills. The classical scholars read the question as wonder rather than doubt, noting that he asks how rather than whether, and that no rebuke follows it in the text.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's account of the family of Imran. The episode belongs to an earlier community. It is retold at greater length in a later surah, where the same request is given more of its setting. The Quran supplies no dates. The classical commentaries place the prayer right after what the guardian had been seeing in the sanctuary. That is how this surah orders the two scenes.

keyTerms.note: An interrogative covering manner and origin together. It asks by what route a thing could come about, which is why commentators hear wonder in it rather than a challenge to the promise itself.
An adjective used of a woman or a man who does not conceive, and also of land that yields nothing. It states a settled condition rather than a season of waiting for one.
A demonstrative meaning in that manner. As an answer it declines to explain, pointing back at the promise instead of forward to a mechanism, and that refusal is the whole substance of the reply.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Age was guessed at rather than counted in Arabia. A man was old when he could no longer ride or work a season through. Not being able to bear children was named openly and carried public weight. A household with no children lost its labour, its defence and its claim on the future. Saying both facts aloud in a prayer was stating what everyone around him already knew.
studies.didYouKnow: The same question, in almost the same words, appears twice in this surah within a few ayat. Once from an old man. Once from a young woman. In both places the reply opens with the same pointing word. The parallel is close enough that the classical scholars regularly discuss the two scenes together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a prophet ask how without the question counting against him. It separates asking for a mechanism from doubting a promise, and answers the first by setting it aside. The reply also grounds the event in will rather than in capacity. The point is not that God can get past barrenness. It is that what he wills is simply done, which takes the obstacle out of the picture.

crossReferences.why: Retells the same exchange, adding that God had created him before when he was nothing.
Puts the same question in Mary's mouth a few ayat later, and answers it the same way.
Shows Abraham's wife asking how she could bear a child in old age, and receiving a like reply.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often your first response to good news is to work out how it could possibly happen. That instinct is not faithlessness; the man here has it too. But watch what it costs you in the minutes afterwards. Try receiving one piece of unexpected good news this week without immediately auditing whether it is plausible.
studies.explainEasier: He asked God how he could have a son. He was old, and his wife could not have children. God told him it would happen anyway, because God does whatever he wants.

studies.title: A Sign Of Three Silent Days
studies.meaning: He asks for a sign and is given one that costs him something. For three days he will not be able to speak to people, only to gesture. Early scholars note that the limit covers speech to people, not speech to God. The same breath tells him to remember his Lord a great deal, and to praise at both ends of the day. So the sign and the instruction are one thing. A tongue taken out of conversation and handed to something else.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's retelling of the family of Imran. The episode belongs to an earlier community. A longer version appears in a later surah. It reports the same three days and adds that he came out to his people and signalled to them. The Quran gives no place or date. The classical scholars discuss the nature of the silence and mostly treat it as an inability, not a choice he made.

keyTerms.note: A word for a signal made with the eyes, lips or hand and without sound. It names communication stripped of voice, which is precisely the sign: he can still be understood, but not heard.
The verb covers keeping in mind and saying aloud at once. Arabic does not separate the two, so remembering God is already a spoken act, which is why it survives the ban on speaking to people.
A noun for the first part of the day, paired here with the late afternoon. Naming the two edges of a day is an Arabic way of saying throughout it, without listing what lies between them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's standing in seventh-century Arabia rested on his speech. He argued his claims aloud. He made contracts by word in front of witnesses. He defended his family's name in public. Poetry and speech-making were the known tools of power. Losing the use of the tongue for three days was not a small private nuisance. It cut him off from every means by which men in that world acted.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places in the Quran where a sign that was asked for arrives as a limit rather than a display. The three days are reported the same way in the longer retelling in a later surah. That is one of several details that match across the two accounts. The two differ a lot in length and stress.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The sign given here works by taking away. It does not show power by adding something to the world. It withdraws a power and leaves the man with only the use of it that matters. So the sign cannot be pulled apart from a discipline. The pairing suggests that a confirmation and an instruction can arrive as one event. It also treats speech to God and speech to people as genuinely different acts.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same sign in a fuller retelling, showing him signalling to his people afterwards.
Shows Abraham asking to be shown, and answered with an action rather than an argument.
Repeats the same instruction: remember God much, and praise Him morning and evening.

studies.applyIt: Try one meal, or one commute, without speaking and without a screen. Not as an achievement, simply as an experiment. Notice what your attention does when its usual outlet is closed. The instruction attached to these three days was not merely to be quiet but to redirect, and the second part is what most people leave out.
studies.explainEasier: He asked God for a sign. God told him he would not be able to talk to people for three days, only make signs with his hands. He was also told to remember God a lot, evening and morning.

studies.title: Chosen And Told To Bow
studies.meaning: Two announcements are made and then an instruction follows. The angels tell Mary she has been chosen, purified, and chosen again over the women of the world. Early scholars discuss the repeat. Most read the first choosing as her acceptance into dedicated service, and the second as her selection for what is about to be announced. Then, straight after that height of honour, comes a command to devotion, to bowing down and to kneeling with others. The honour does not excuse her from the ordinary posture.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. These ayat belong to the surah's central story, and to its conversation with a community that honours Mary deeply. The passage names her choosing in strong terms. Then it places her among worshippers rather than above them. The Quran reports the words of the angels without describing a setting. The classical commentaries add no occasion beyond the order of the surah itself.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to take the pure part of a thing. It is used twice in one ayah of the same person, which the commentators generally read as two distinct selections rather than emphasis alone.
An imperative from the root for sustained obedient standing, the same word used earlier in this surah of the reverent. It names a posture held over time rather than an act completed once.
The verb for bending at the waist. Its command form here is addressed to a woman on her own, while the phrase immediately following places her among a plural group of those bowing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Distinction in Arabian society came with exemptions. A chief was not expected to carry water; a man of standing sent others to do what was beneath him, and honour was measured partly by what you no longer had to do yourself. Rank meant relief from common tasks. The instruction here runs directly against that grain, attaching honour to joining in rather than to being excused.
studies.didYouKnow: Mary is the only woman the Quran addresses by name in direct speech. This passage does it twice, in two ayat in a row. The surah that carries her name is one of only a handful named after a person. And it is the one surah in the Quran named for a woman.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being chosen and being bound are joined here, not traded off. Being chosen above all women is followed at once by an instruction to do what every worshipper does, and to do it in company. That puts the highest honour the passage can name inside ordinary devotion, not beyond it. The purifying is described as done to her. So even her standing stays a gift rather than an achievement.

crossReferences.why: Names Mary again as one of the devout, using the same root as the command given here.
Places her withdrawn to an eastern place, supplying the setting this passage leaves out.
Supplies the dedication and upbringing that brought her to the point of this address.

studies.applyIt: Think of an area where you have some standing, at work, in a family, in a community. Find one ordinary task there that people at your level usually stop doing. Do it this week without announcing it. This passage attaches the highest honour it can name to bowing alongside other people rather than in front of them.
studies.explainEasier: The angels told Mary that God had chosen her and made her pure. He chose her above all the women in the world. Then they told her to worship her Lord, and to bow and kneel with the others.

studies.title: You Were Not There
studies.meaning: The story pauses to speak to the one receiving it. These accounts belong to what is unseen. The point is made by two denials. You were not there when they cast lots over who would take charge of Mary. You were not there when they quarrelled about it. The classical scholars note the choice of detail. Not a miracle, but a dispute over who would take responsibility for a child. That is exactly the sort of thing an outsider would have no way of knowing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, breaking into the account of Mary between her upbringing and the announcement of her son. Addresses of this kind appear all through the Quran wherever a story from an earlier community is retold. Here the break lands inside a surah in conversation with people who held those histories themselves. So the claim being made is about where the account comes from, not about what it says.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for news that carries consequence, distinguished by the lexicographers from ordinary information. It names accounts that change something for whoever receives them.
What is absent from perception, whether hidden by time, distance or nature. The word does not mean the supernatural; a past event no witness survives is unseen in precisely this sense.
The word for a trimmed reed used in writing, and here for the marked shafts cast to settle a question. One object served both purposes, which is why the term carries so much at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Casting marked arrows or reeds to decide a matter was familiar across pre-Islamic Arabia. It was used at sanctuaries to settle questions nobody could otherwise resolve. Everyone hearing this ayah would have known the procedure at once. It gave a decision the look of being fair to all sides. That is exactly what a group of men arguing over a costly duty would have wanted.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran often marks the edge of the Prophet's own knowledge with the phrase you were not there. It uses it of Moses at the mountain, of Joseph's brothers agreeing on their plan, and here. The formula appears across several surahs. It always attaches to a small, checkable circumstance, never to a grand event.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The claim rests on a detail rather than on a marvel, which is a particular kind of argument. Anybody could invent a miracle. Few would think to invent a quarrel over guardianship. The passage also defines the unseen widely enough to take in the ordinary past. That puts revelation in the place of a witness rather than a reader of meaning. And it does so without running down the accounts already held nearby.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same formula: you were not with them when they agreed upon their plan.
Repeats it of Moses, saying the Prophet was not present on the mountain's western side.
Calls the account of Noah news of the unseen, revealed and not previously known.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you know rests on testimony rather than sight: your own birth, your grandparents' lives, nearly all of history. You already live by trusted report. Pick one thing you are certain of today and trace how you actually came to know it. The exercise makes this ayah's kind of claim less foreign than it first looks.
studies.explainEasier: These stories come from things you could not have seen. You were not there when they drew lots to decide who would look after Mary. You were not there when they argued about it either.

studies.title: A Word From Him
studies.meaning: The angels choose every word with care. He is a word from God. His name comes with a title and with his mother's name, not a father's. He is held in high regard in this world and the next, and among those brought near. Then two moments of his speech are named: in the cradle and in grown-up years. Early scholars read a word from God to mean brought into being by God's command. They also treat the naming through his mother as part of the announcement itself.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is Medinan. It speaks closely to the Christian community of Najran. Classical sources report that their delegation travelled to Medina to discuss this very question. The surah does not open with disagreement. It gives the announcement first, and gives it in terms of honour. Only later in the chapter does it discuss how he is to be understood, once the story has been laid out.

keyTerms.note: A title, not a name. Its root means to wipe or to anoint. The Quran always uses it of Jesus. Early scholars discuss several possible roots for it and do not settle on one.
From the word for a face. It describes a person whose face is welcome, someone of standing whose word carries weight. The ayah extends that standing to this world and the next alike.
A passive form: they are drawn close, rather than coming near by their own power. It names a rank set by nearness to God, and the ayah describes that rank as given rather than earned.
The word for the age between youth and old age, roughly the middle years. Pairing it with the cradle marks the two ends of his speaking: one of them impossible, one entirely ordinary.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names in Arabia carried fathers. A man was known as the son of his father, and that chain placed him in a tribe, an inheritance and a set of obligations. To name a child by his mother in a formal announcement was unusual enough to be a statement in itself. It fixed his identity in a way the audience could not mishear, and it has stayed attached to him since.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran calls Jesus the son of Mary more than twenty times. The phrase became the standard Arabic way of naming him. Naming a man by his mother was rare in that setting. Yet the usage holds across surahs sent down years apart, in very different circumstances.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The announcement sets out his standing in the strongest terms it has. Every part of that standing is placed in what he was given. He is a word from God. He is brought near rather than approaching. He is held in regard in both worlds. The passage places him without lowering him. It honours him fully, and keeps him on the created side throughout. That is how the surah frames the discussion that comes later.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same terms of him, a word conveyed to Mary and a spirit from Him.
Reports the speech from the cradle, in which he names himself a servant of God.
Compares his creation to Adam's later in this surah, as made from dust by a command.

studies.applyIt: Read the announcement slowly and notice how much honour it gives. If you have Christian friends or family, it is worth knowing well. It is neither a put-down nor a full agreement. Saying clearly what your own book says about Jesus helps more in a conversation than a rough sense picked up from either side.
studies.explainEasier: Angels bring Mary good news. She will have a son named Jesus. God has given him a high place in this life and the next. As a baby in his crib he will speak to people.

studies.title: Be, And It Is
studies.meaning: Mary asks the same question the old man asked a few ayat earlier. The reply differs in one telling word. He was told that God does what He wills. She is told that God creates what He wills. Then the answer gives a mechanism after all: a command, and the thing is. Early scholars note that this formula is used in the Quran for events with no precedent. The passage then names what the child will be taught. That places him inside a tradition of learning, not outside it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and part of the surah's central story and its careful account of how the birth is to be understood. Classical sources link this section to a Christian delegation from Najran, then in Medina. The Quran's order is deliberate. How the creation happens is stated before any disagreement is raised. The teaching of the Torah and the Gospel is named in the same breath as the miracle.

keyTerms.note: The verb for bringing something into being with a form. It replaces the broader verb used in the answer to Zechariah. Early scholars read that swap as marking a difference between the two births.
A two-letter imperative, the shortest command Arabic can make. Its brevity is the point: no process is described between the word and the thing, so nothing stands between the will and the result.
Set apart here from the Book, so it names more than a text: sound judgement about how and when to act. The root also carries restraint, as of a bridle holding a horse.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Making anything in that world took time you could watch. A garment was spun, woven and cut over weeks; a house went up course by course; a field waited on rain and then on months. Nothing came into being without a visible process attached to it. A creation with no interval between the word and the result was, in that setting, unlike everything the audience had ever seen made.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula in which God says Be, and a thing is, occurs eight times in the Quran. It is used of the making of the heavens and the earth, of the raising of the dead, and here of one birth. The same short phrase covers events of very different scale. Early scholars treat that as deliberate, not accidental.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage takes a unique event and sets it inside a general rule. It does not treat it as an exception. Creation by command is God's ordinary way of working. So this birth is unusual in its circumstances, not in how it happens. The teaching named right afterwards works the same way. Whatever is singular about him, his learning is described in the terms used of other prophets.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical formula of the heavens and the earth, originated with no precedent before them.
Applies the same command to Adam, created from dust, as this surah's own comparison.
States the principle in general: His command, when He wills a thing, is to say Be.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between a question asked in order to understand and one asked in order to resist. Mary asks how, and receives an answer. Think of something you have been told is possible and have quietly filed as unrealistic. Ask yourself honestly which of the two kinds of question you have been putting to it, and answer without softening.
studies.explainEasier: Mary asks how she can have a baby when no man has touched her. God tells her that He makes whatever He wants. He only has to say Be, and the thing is there.

studies.title: By God's Leave
studies.meaning: A messenger describes his own signs, and each one carries a limit. He shapes a bird from clay and it lives. He heals two conditions that medicine could not reach. He brings the dead back to life. He tells people what they have eaten and what they store at home. Three times the phrase by God's leave breaks into the list. Early scholars point out that he says it himself, about himself. The limit belongs to the claim. It is not added later.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's account of Jesus and his mission to the Children of Israel. The signs are reported as given, with no order of dates attached. Early commentaries note that each one answered something the community of that time prized. They treat the pattern as general. Every messenger is described as given signs the people of his own moment could recognise.

keyTerms.note: From a root that also means to hear or give ear. In Arabic, permission is granted by listening. So the phrase implies an authority present and allowing, not just a rule that permits.
A specific word for blindness present from birth, not acquired later. Naming it on its own rules out any recovery that might be credited to the passage of time or to treatment.
A noun for outward shape and appearance. It says carefully that what he makes has the form of a bird. Early scholars note that this marks the line between shaping a thing and giving it life.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medicine in the ancient world mostly meant making room. A blind man was led about. A person with a skin disease lived apart. Families built their lives around conditions nobody expected to change. Healers set bones and mixed remedies for fevers. Nothing in daily life turned back a condition a person was born with. That is why these two were the ones named.
studies.didYouKnow: The sign of the clay bird appears twice in the Quran: here, and in a later surah where God recounts the same favours directly to Jesus. Both times the phrase by God's leave is attached to it. The Quran mentions the sign nowhere else, and never once without that qualification in place.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a messenger hold great signs and give away their source in the same sentence. That settles a tension the surah is working on. Honour and power can be given freely, as long as their origin stays clear. The limit is repeated three times inside one short speech. That repetition does the work an argument would otherwise have to do, and it does it in his own voice.

crossReferences.why: Recounts the same signs, with God addressing Jesus and repeating the same qualification each time.
Continues the same speech, ending on God as my Lord and your Lord.
Says Jesus was given clear signs and supported by the holy spirit.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are genuinely good at, the thing people come to you for. Say aloud, once, where the capacity for it came from. Not as false modesty; the man speaking here does not understate what he can do. He simply never makes a sentence about it without naming the source, and that is a habit rather than a mood.
studies.explainEasier: Jesus tells his people about the signs God gave him. He can shape a bird from clay and make it live. He can heal the blind and raise the dead. Each time he says it happens by God's leave.

studies.title: My Lord And Your Lord
studies.meaning: The speech now turns to its purpose. He confirms the scripture they already hold. He says that some of what was forbidden is now made lawful. He points again at the sign he brought. Then the whole message shrinks to one sentence: God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. Early scholars note the order of the pronouns. The speaker puts himself under that lordship before he addresses anyone else. They read the closing phrase as the meaning of a straight path.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the surah's account of Jesus, and central to its conversation with a community that honoured him. The passage reports his own words rather than describing him from outside. Classical sources link this section with a delegation from Najran. The Quran's method here is to quote, not to argue. Reported speech carries a point the surah states directly only later.

keyTerms.note: The same participle used of the Quran at this surah's opening. Applying it to a messenger and to a book alike presents both as witnesses to what came before them, not as replacements for it.
An idiom for what lies ahead in place and behind in time, so what came earlier stands in front of a person. Arabic pictures the past as visible and the future as somewhere behind the back.
A road broad enough for many to travel, paired with a participle meaning standing upright and holding its direction. The phrase names both the way and its refusal to bend away from it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Roads in that world were not built; they were worn by use. A straight route between two places was rare, since paths bent around wells, rock, and territory a traveller could not safely cross. A way that held its direction was the exception and was known by name. Anyone who had made a long journey knew the difference between the shortest road and the one people actually took.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered a straight path occurs more than thirty times in the Quran. That includes the short surah every reciter opens with. Here it is placed in the mouth of an earlier prophet, describing his own message. It is one of several spots where the wording of that opening chapter turns up inside a story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The speech puts the speaker and his listeners on the same side of one bond. It does this in the grammar of the sentence, by naming his Lord before theirs. The central claim is settled without being set out as a plain statement. Lifting some earlier rules works the same way. It shows that revelation can change in its details while its centre holds. That is the surah's larger case for what carries over.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same sentence from him almost word for word, in a later surah's account.
Repeats it again as his own speech, adding that this is a straight path.
Asks for the same path, in the prayer that every recitation of the Quran begins with.

studies.applyIt: Notice the order of the pronouns: my Lord, then your Lord. When you next find yourself telling someone what they ought to do about faith, try putting yourself into the sentence first, and honestly. It changes what you say next. Most religious advice fails at exactly this point, before any of its content is even reached.
studies.explainEasier: Jesus tells his people that he agrees with the book they already have. He says that God is his Lord and their Lord too. So they should worship God. That, he says, is the straight path.

studies.title: Who Will Stand With Me
studies.meaning: The turn is described as something felt: he sensed disbelief. He does not press the argument further. Instead he asks a question that makes people name themselves. The disciples answer in three parts. We are the helpers. We have believed. Bear witness that we have submitted. Early scholars note the call for witness at the end. It turns a private belief into something said aloud in front of others, which is what that moment needed.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the point where the surah's account of Jesus turns from his mission to how it was received. The episode is told again in a later surah, where the same word for his helpers appears. The Quran gives no setting and names no one. Early commentaries treat this as the moment the community around him split. That is why the surah places it just before a plan and a counter-plan.

keyTerms.note: A verb tied to the physical senses rather than to reasoning. It suggests he felt the change in the room before anyone stated it, which is how opposition usually announces itself first.
The plural of a word for one who comes to another's aid in difficulty. The same word later named the people of Medina who received the emigrants, a resonance the first audience heard at once.
A term the early Arabic dictionary writers connect with whiteness and with purity or sincerity. The Quran uses it only of this group, and its exact root is discussed without ever being settled.
The participle from the same root this surah uses for the religion God accepts. Placing it in the disciples' mouths ties them directly to the definition given earlier in the chapter.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a tribal society, declaring support was a formal act with consequences. Standing up for a man under pressure meant taking on his enemies as your own. It was done in the open, so everyone knew where duties now lay. A quiet well-wisher gave nothing at all. The question here follows that pattern. It does not ask what people think. It asks who will say so.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the disciples use for helpers is the one that gave the people of Medina their historical name. The surah's first listeners carried that name themselves. Putting it in the mouths of a much older community links the two groups across centuries, through a single choice of wording.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats faith as something that has to be sayable. Belief is stated, and then witness is asked for. The inward and the spoken are held together, and neither stands on its own. The passage also shows a prophet meeting rejection by looking for company rather than by raising the argument. What follows in the surah confirms that the answer given here was the thing that lasted.

crossReferences.why: Recalls the same exchange and calls the believers to be helpers as the disciples were.
Reports the disciples' declaration again, with God saying He inspired them to believe.
Gives their prayer immediately afterwards, asking to be recorded among the witnesses.

studies.applyIt: Support that stays private is not much use to the person who needs it. Think of someone currently taking heat for something you actually agree with. Say so to them directly this week, in a message they can keep. Not a public post. The question in this passage asks who will stand up, and it expects a name in reply.
studies.explainEasier: Jesus could feel that people were turning against him. So he asked who would stand with him and help. His close followers said they would. They said they believed in God and had given themselves to him.

studies.title: Count Us Among The Witnesses
studies.meaning: A short prayer is followed by a sentence that reverses the scene. The disciples ask to be written among those who bear witness, having named what they believed and whom they followed. Then, with no transition, the passage says that they schemed and God schemed. The same word is used of both, and the commentators explain that of God it means the undoing of a plot by an unseen arrangement, not deception. The contrast is between a plan made in a room and one that encloses it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's account of the reception Jesus met. The Quran neither describes the plan nor names those who made it. The classical commentaries connect the passage to a plot against his life and to the outcome the following ayat report, on which they preserve more than one reading. The surah keeps the account brief here because its concern is the pattern rather than the sequence of events.

keyTerms.note: The verb for recording in writing. Asking to be written among a group is asking for enrolment on a list, an image drawn from the registers kept of tribes, of soldiers, and of shares.
Those who testify to what they have seen, and in another usage those present at an event. Both senses fit: they ask to be counted among people who were there and who then said so.
A verb for a plan made out of its target's sight. Of people it carries blame. Of God, early scholars explain it as the hidden overturning of a scheme, keeping the mirrored wording without the blame.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Registers mattered in the seventh century. Tribes kept lists of who was owed a share, who had ridden out on a raid, and who stood surety for a debt. Being written down was how a claim survived memory and argument. To ask God to write your name among a group was to reach for the most concrete image of belonging available, one everyone had watched decided in practice.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here of scheming is applied to God several times in the Quran. It always mirrors a word just used of people in the same sentence. Classical writers on style describe this as a known device, in which a term is turned back on an opponent. They note that the Quran never uses the word of God on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat placed together say something this surah repeats elsewhere. A group states its loyalty and asks to be written down. Meanwhile a plan is already moving against them. The passage does not answer that with a promise of safety. It says that the larger arrangement holds the smaller one inside it. That changes what the plan means, without always stopping it from running.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same mirrored wording of a plot laid against the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him).
Shows a scheme made and its outcome reversed, using the same vocabulary throughout.
Shows others asking to be written among the witnesses, in almost identical words.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between asking to be safe and asking to be counted. This prayer asks for the second. Think about which of the two you actually ask for, most days. Then say the disciples' request once in your own words, and notice that it contains no request for the situation to improve.
studies.explainEasier: The followers of Jesus pray to God. They ask to be counted among the people who tell the truth about what they saw. Others made a secret plan against him. But God had a plan too.

studies.title: Raising You To Me
studies.meaning: God speaks to Jesus directly and states four things. A taking. A raising. A clearing from those who refused him. And a placing of his followers above them until the Resurrection. The first word is the hard one. Scholars differ over whether it means causing to die, taking in full, or taking up as one is taken in sleep. The classical commentaries record that whole range and do not force a choice. The ayah then leaves every remaining dispute to God's own judgement.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and closely tied to the surah's dealings with the Christian community of Najran. Classical sources report their delegation coming to Medina. The passage does not narrate the events around the end of his earthly presence. It states what God did, then leaves the disagreement open. That is the method the whole section uses. State the essentials, and leave the disputed detail to the judgement named at the close.

keyTerms.note: A participle from a root meaning to receive something in full, used both of collecting a debt and of death. Early scholars record several readings of it in this place and settle on none.
The participle for lifting up, used in the Quran of rank as well as of place. Both senses appear in the commentaries, and the word itself does not choose between them.
From the root for purity, here in the sense of separating someone from what would stain them. It concerns his standing among people rather than any condition within him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man's name in Arabia could outlive him. Whoever told his story afterwards could repair it or ruin it. Poets were paid to praise and paid to insult. A family's standing turned on which account survived. Clearing a man of those who had wronged his name was a known act in that world. It mattered as much as anything done to his body.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah leaves a disagreement to a later judgement rather than settling it. The Quran makes that move often with matters disputed between communities. The wording appears in several surahs. The clause about judging between people over what they differed in nearly always comes at the close of such a question, not in the middle.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage guards a prophet's honour without settling the historical question that divides communities. It says what God did with him. It says the dispute itself will be judged. That shape suggests how believers might hold such questions in the meantime. Open where the sources are open. Settled only where the text is plain.

crossReferences.why: Addresses the same contested end more directly, and says God raised him to Himself.
Uses the same verb for taking, in the account of Jesus answering on the Day of Judgement.
Ends another dispute between communities the same way, by deferring it to God's judgement.

studies.applyIt: There are questions you will not settle, including some that matter. This ayah models what to do with them: state clearly what you do hold, name the disagreement as a disagreement, and leave the verdict where it belongs. Try that phrasing once this week on something you have been arguing about in circles.
studies.explainEasier: God tells Jesus that He will take him and lift him up to Himself. He will clear him of the people who refused him. On the last day God will settle what they argued about.

studies.title: In This World And The Next
studies.meaning: The sentence begun in the last ayah splits into two outcomes. This is the first of them. The punishment is described as reaching both worlds. The closing clause rules out anyone stepping in. Early scholars note the pairing of the two worlds, which returns across this surah. They read the phrase about helpers as a denial of the very thing an Arabian audience would look for first. Not innocence, but someone with enough standing to speak up for you before God.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It closes the surah's account of Jesus. Next comes the passage that compares his creation to Adam's. The wording repeats a phrase used earlier in this surah of a different group. Early commentaries note this habit of returning to its own phrasing. The passage speaks about a group marked out by refusal. It does not speak about any named people or time.

keyTerms.note: A particle that introduces one branch of a division and expects a matching branch to follow. Its presence signals that the sentence is only half finished, and the next ayah supplies the other half.
The plural of one who comes to another's aid, from the same root used a few ayat earlier of the disciples. The word that named loyalty in one scene names its absence in this one.
The adjective comes from a root meaning to tighten or bind hard. It describes intensity as constriction rather than as duration, which is a different image from the one the English suggests.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Nobody in Arabia stood alone before a claim. When a man was accused, his clan bargained and the elders stepped in. Blood money was raised by relatives who might not even like him. Guilt rarely met a person head on, because a network took the shock. Saying that someone has no helpers described a state almost unthinkable in that world. It was worse than the penalty itself.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase about having no helpers occurs earlier in this same surah. It comes there in a passage about those who kill prophets and those who call for justice. The surah uses the formula twice, in two quite different sections. It is one of many repeats that bind its long argument across changes of subject.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places consequence in both worlds rather than putting all of it off. That keeps the present morally serious. Its sharpest clause is the last one. What is taken away is not comfort but anyone to speak on your behalf. That says something about how answering for what you do is shaped here. The decisive absence is not of pleasure. It is of anyone standing between a person and what they did.

crossReferences.why: Uses the identical closing phrase about having no helpers, earlier in this surah.
Supplies the matching branch of the sentence: the reward given in full to the faithful.
Denies that intercession will be accepted or any help given on that day.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your sense of safety comes from people who would step in for you: a manager, a relative, a friend with influence. That is real and worth being grateful for. Name one of them today and thank them. Then sit for a moment with the fact that the arrangement is temporary, which is what this ayah is pointing at.
studies.explainEasier: God says that people who turn away from the truth will be punished. It will happen in this life and the next. No one will be able to help them or stand up for them.

studies.title: Wages Paid In Full
studies.meaning: The other branch of the sentence arrives. Those who believed and worked righteousness are paid their wages in full, using the same commercial verb the surah applied earlier to the settling of every account. Then a clause is attached that seems to belong to the first branch rather than this one: God does not love the wrongdoers. Commentators read the placement as deliberate, so that even a promise of reward closes on a limit. The next ayah names what has just been recited.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the close of the surah's account of Jesus. It sits just before the comparison with Adam. The second ayah steps outside the story to describe it. Classical commentaries link that to the talks then going on in Medina with a visiting Christian delegation. Naming the recitation as verses and as a reminder frames what came before as evidence. It is not a story told for its own sake.

keyTerms.note: The commercial verb for discharging an obligation completely, used earlier in this surah of the final reckoning. Applied to reward, it makes the promise a settlement rather than a present.
The word for a worker's pay, not for a gift. It implies something earned and owed, which is why the verb of full payment suits it and why the two words are so often paired.
Two words: a reminder that brings something back to mind, and an adjective from the root for firm judgement. Together they name a text that recalls and decides in the same breath.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Paid work existed alongside slavery and family duty in seventh-century Arabia. Men were hired for a harvest, a journey, or a season of herding. The pay was agreed first and settled at the end. Fights over a withheld wage were common enough to be a known kind of grievance. Full payment on the agreed day was hoped for rather than assumed.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming this recitation as verses and a wise reminder occurs only here in the Quran. The surah places it at a hinge. It comes right after a long story and right before a comparison drawn from it. This is one of several points where the text pauses to describe itself in the middle of an argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reward is described in the words of wages, not of favour. That makes it owed rather than merely hoped for. The closing clause holds the whole promise inside a moral frame. The second ayah then does what this surah does again and again. It names its own material. The story just told is called a sign and a reminder, so its purpose is stated rather than left to be guessed.

crossReferences.why: Supplies the other branch of this divided sentence, the outcome for those who refuse.
Uses the same promise of wages paid in full, adding an increase from God's bounty.
Says the patient will be given their reward without any reckoning applied to it.

studies.applyIt: Think about work you have done that was never acknowledged, and notice the small resentment attached to it. The word used here is wages, not gifts. Try holding one unacknowledged thing this week as already owed and already recorded, and see whether that changes how badly you need someone else to notice it.
studies.explainEasier: God says that people who believe and do good will get their full pay for it. Nothing will be held back. Then God says that what has just been read out are His own signs and a wise reminder.

studies.title: The Likeness Of Adam
studies.meaning: The argument is made by comparison, not by denial. Suppose a birth without a father shows something extraordinary about a person's nature. Then the first human being, made without either parent, would show more. The comparison works by scale. Whatever is unusual in one case is more unusual in the other. No tradition has drawn that conclusion about Adam. The next ayah closes the matter briefly. It names the truth as from God and warns against wavering.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical sources link this section to the Christian delegation from Najran, who came to Medina to discuss the nature of Jesus. The comparison belongs to that conversation. The surah has already given the announcement of his birth in terms of full honour. So the argument arrives after the honour rather than in place of it. The commentaries stress that order.

keyTerms.note: Not a metaphor but a parallel case put forward for reasoning. The word introduces an argument by analogy, which is how early scholars read this ayah as a whole.
The most ordinary material named in the Quran's accounts of human origin. Choosing it strengthens the point, since the more unusual creation began from the least remarkable substance available.
From a root associated with drawing back and forth, as milk is drawn from an udder. It pictures doubt as an oscillation rather than as a settled position a person has arrived at.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Argument by parallel case was the ordinary tool of Arabian dispute. A poet or a judge made his point by setting one situation beside another. He then let the audience draw the line themselves. That was held to work better than stating the point outright. The form of this ayah would have felt familiar at once, even where its content was fought over.
studies.didYouKnow: The command Be, and it is, appears twice within thirteen ayat of this surah. It is used once of Jesus and once of Adam. Those are the only two places the formula occurs in the whole chapter. Their pairing across such a short distance is the hinge this comparison turns on.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats an unusual origin as evidence about God, not about the one created. Creation by command is God's ordinary way of working. So the way a person came into being says nothing about their nature. The principle is applied to one question here. Its reach is wider. It cuts the worth and standing of a human being loose from the circumstances of their arrival.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same command of Jesus twelve ayat earlier, which is what makes the comparison land.
Describes Adam's creation from clay, and the breathing of spirit into him.
Addresses the same question directly, asking that nothing beyond the truth be said in religion.

studies.applyIt: The move this ayah makes is worth borrowing. Rather than deny a claim, it sets a second case beside it and lets the comparison do the work. Next time you disagree with someone, try finding the parallel case instead of the counter-argument. It is slower, and it leaves the other person somewhere to stand.
studies.explainEasier: God says that Jesus is like Adam. God made Adam out of dust. Then He said Be, and Adam was there. Adam had no father and no mother at all.

studies.title: Come, Let Us Call
studies.meaning: When argument has run out, a different kind of settlement is proposed. Both sides are to bring their families and stand together. Then they call down God's rejection on whichever side is lying. What is staked is the striking part. Not property, not standing, but the people each side most wants to protect. Early scholars record that the invocation never took place. The other party declined it and chose a negotiated settlement instead. The sources treat that refusal as telling in itself.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. This is among the best attested occasions in the surah. Classical sources agree that a Christian delegation from Najran came to Medina. They discussed the nature of Jesus at length. When the discussion reached its limit, they were offered this shared invocation. The delegation stepped back from it and negotiated terms instead. The Quran records the offer, not the outcome.

keyTerms.note: From a root suggesting release and unrestrained supplication, used of praying with nothing held back. The form makes it mutual, an appeal both parties make together rather than one against the other.
The plural of the word for a self or soul. Read plainly it names each party's own persons, and early scholars discuss how widely its scope extends without reaching one settled answer.
Those who state what they know to be false, as distinct from those who are merely mistaken. The proposal targets deliberate falsehood, which is why sincerity on both sides is its condition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Oaths were the final instrument of Arabian dispute. Where evidence failed, a man swore. How serious an oath was depended on what he put at risk in swearing it. An oath taken with children present placed the whole family under whatever followed. This proposal uses that known procedure and raises it to the most serious form available.
studies.didYouKnow: The invocation described here is one of the few proposals in the Quran that classical sources agree was never carried out. For early scholars the interest lies in the withdrawal, not in any event. A party sure of its position declined a test. It had been invited to help set the terms of that test.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts the weight of a religious claim in what a person will stake on it. That is not an argument about evidence. It is an argument about sincerity. It assumes both sides truly believe that God answers. The passage also sets a limit on arguing itself. Once knowledge has come, more argument is not the reply. What is offered instead is a proposal that would end the matter.

crossReferences.why: Sets out a comparable procedure of solemn invocation where ordinary evidence cannot settle a matter.
Puts a similar challenge to another community: wish for death, if you are truthful.
Gives the earlier instruction for the same situation, that the duty ends at conveying.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between believing something and being willing to stake something on it. You do not need a dramatic test for this. Ask what you would actually risk on one conviction you state often, and answer honestly. If the answer turns out to be nothing, that is worth knowing before somebody else discovers it.
studies.explainEasier: Some people kept arguing about Jesus even after the truth had come. God gave them a way to settle it. Both sides should bring their families and stand together. Then they should ask God to turn away from whichever side is lying.

studies.title: The Narrative Of Truth
studies.meaning: The long account closes with a summary in three parts. What has been told is the true narrative; there is no god but God; and God is mighty and wise. The order matters, because the story is presented as leading to the statement rather than decorating it. Then a short conditional follows: if they turn away, God knows those who corrupt. Classical commentators note that the response to refusal is knowledge rather than punishment, which leaves the matter where it began.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the end of the surah's story about Mary and Jesus. It comes just before the well-known invitation to a word held in common. Classical sources place this whole sequence in the discussions with the delegation from Najran. Its position matters. The summary comes after a long and honouring account, and before an appeal. It does not come at the end of a rebuke.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to follow a track. A narrative in Arabic is literally a following of traces, so calling this the true account claims accurate tracking rather than merely honest intention.
From a root meaning to be scarce and therefore precious, and also strong and hard to reach. It combines value with inaccessibility, which is why English needs two words to carry it.
From a root meaning spoilage, used of food going bad and of an arrangement breaking down. It names damage done to something that was working, rather than wrongdoing in the abstract.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Family lines and tribal history were passed on by specialists. Their standing rested on getting it right. A reciter caught inventing lost that standing for good. Arabic grew a set of technical words for judging how sound a chain of transmission was. To call an account the true narrative there was to make a claim the audience knew how to test.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for narrative gives its name to a later surah. The Quran also uses it of the story of Joseph, calling that the most beautiful of accounts. The root's basic sense is following a track. It gives the verb used when the sister of Moses is told to follow her brother along the river.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage puts a story and a statement of belief in one sentence. An account of a family and two births is offered as an argument for God's oneness, not as a picture of it. The closing clause is just as careful. Refusal is met with a statement about God's knowledge. That permits no human response. It leaves the judging where this surah always puts it.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately with the invitation to a word held in common between communities.
Calls the account of Joseph the most beautiful of narratives, using this same word.
Closes Abraham's prayer with the same two names, mighty and wise, set side by side.

studies.applyIt: Try telling one story about your own life today in a way that ends where it actually leads, rather than where it is most flattering to stop. This ayah closes a long narrative with the single claim the narrative was for. Most of us let stories trail off. Notice what yours would have to end on.
studies.explainEasier: This is the true story, God says, and there is only one God. He is strong and wise. If people turn away from that, God knows who is breaking things and spoiling them.

studies.title: Come To A Common Word
studies.meaning: An invitation is issued rather than an argument won. The proposal is limited to three things: worship of God alone, joining nothing with Him, and no one among us taking others as lords beside God. That third clause turns the invitation inward as well as outward. It names a failure any community can fall into. If the invitation is declined, the reply given is not a rebuke. It is a statement of your own position.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. Classical sources report this ayah in the letters sent to rulers beyond Arabia. The wording appears in the letter to the Byzantine emperor kept in the early collections. Others connect it to the delegation from Najran that came to Medina to debate with the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). The two settings fit together, and early scholars generally report both.

keyTerms.note: The adjective means level or even, from the root for equality. It describes ground on which neither party stands higher, which is why the invitation cannot be read as a demand for submission.

The plural of the word used for God as Lord, here applied to human beings. It covers anyone whose word is treated as final, which is why early scholars read the clause as addressed to everyone present.
An imperative addressed to the ones declining. Instead of arguing further, the speaker asks them to be witnesses to his own position, which converts an opponent into a record keeper.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Diplomacy in that world ran on formal letters, memorised and carried by a single trusted rider, sometimes for weeks. They were read aloud to a court.
