A message had to state its business in one or two sentences. A messenger had to be able to repeat it, and a hostile audience could not easily twist it. This ayah has exactly that shape. It is short, quotable, and framed so that refusing it costs the refuser more than the sender.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for a common word has had an unusually long public life. In 2007 it was chosen as the title of an open letter from Muslim scholars to Christian leaders. The name came straight from this ayah. The letters that followed became one of the most widely read documents of modern exchange between faiths. Early scholars had already read the ayah as a model for address rather than dispute.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The invitation names the least you can agree on, and refuses to inflate it. That is a discipline, not a concession. Including the clause about taking one another as lords puts the speaker under the same test as the person addressed. And the instruction for what to say when refused sets the terms of disagreement. State your position, ask for it to be witnessed, and stop.

crossReferences.why: Instructs argument with the People of the Book in the best manner, on shared ground.
Sets out the method: invite with wisdom and good instruction, and argue in the better way.
Gives a parallel declaration: our deeds are ours, yours are yours, and God will gather us.

studies.applyIt: In your next disagreement about belief, start by naming out loud what you and the other person actually agree on. Say it in one sentence, before anything else. Then stop and let them respond to that. The order in this ayah is the whole method. Most conversations of this kind fail because the shared sentence is never said.
studies.explainEasier: The message to Jews and Christians is simple: let us agree on one thing. We all worship God alone. Nobody should treat any other person as if they were God.

studies.title: Arguing About Abraham
studies.meaning: The question is put as a matter of order in time. Abraham lived before either the Torah or the Gospel came down. So a dispute over which later community he belonged to asks what the dates cannot support. The argument is about sequence, not about doctrine. It ends by inviting the listeners to reason it through themselves. Early scholars note the tone. The address is direct, but the reasoning is offered rather than forced on anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. More than one community in and around Medina claimed Abraham. The claim mattered because it carried authority over whose practice was the original. Classical commentaries report disputes of exactly this kind in the city. The surah's answer does not pick between the claimants. It points out that the labels being fought over came into being after the man they are applied to.

keyTerms.note: From the root for advancing a proof. The form used makes it reciprocal, a contest of claims, and the verb recurs several times in this section of the surah as the activity being questioned.
The passive of the verb for revelation descending. Using the passive keeps attention on the timing of the event rather than on who caused it, which is exactly what the argument turns on.
From a root meaning to tie or tether, the same word behind the term for a hobble on a camel. Reason in Arabic is the faculty that restrains, holding a person back from running loose.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Claims about ancestry were fought over in Arabia the way property was, and just as hard. Tribes traced themselves back to famous forebears. A claim that held brought precedence, better marriages, and a share in the care of the sanctuary. Arguments about who a distant ancestor belonged to were not about the past. They settled standing in the present, and everyone listening knew it.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran mentions Abraham in twenty-five different surahs. Only Moses is named more often. This surah names him again and again. He is the figure the Quran most often uses as common ground between communities. That is part of why the argument here is fought over him and not someone else.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a limit on how far a later label can be pushed backwards. A community formed around a revelation cannot claim someone who came before it. That holds even when it truly traces itself to him. The limit protects the earlier figure from being taken over. It also says something wider about identity. What a person was is not settled by who later claims them.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same question about several patriarchs, asking whether you know better than God does.
Gives the conclusion two ayat later, describing what Abraham actually was.
Describes Abraham as a community in himself, upright, and not among those who associate.

studies.applyIt: Notice the shape of this argument: not a better claim, but a question about the timeline. The next time you find yourself in a dispute about who owns a tradition, a phrase, or a founder, check the dates before you weigh the merits. It settles more arguments than people expect, and it costs nothing to look.
studies.explainEasier: God asks the people of earlier books why they argue about Abraham. Their books came long after he lived. So those books cannot tell them which group he was in. God asks them to think it through.

studies.title: Neither One Nor The Other
studies.meaning: A distinction is drawn between two kinds of dispute. There is arguing about what you have some knowledge of, which the ayah notes without endorsing, and arguing about what you have none of, which it questions. Then the answer to the previous ayah comes plainly: Abraham belonged to neither of the later communities. He is described instead by two words, one meaning turned away from every false object of worship, the other meaning surrendered to God. He is not claimed for a third party; he is described.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, carrying on the address begun in the ayah before. The dispute over Abraham was live in Medina. His authority backed claims about whose practice was the original one. Classical commentaries describe the argument in general terms. They read the surah's answer as removing the terms of the dispute rather than deciding it. That is why the description given uses neither community's name.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to lean or turn aside. It describes someone who has turned from every false object of worship toward God, and it was used in Arabia before Islam of individuals who kept to that alone.
The participle from the same root as the religion named earlier in this surah. Applied to a figure who long preceded any later community, it names a disposition rather than a membership.
The indefinite form is used twice, so the ayah speaks of having some knowledge of a matter rather than of expertise in it. That makes the contrast one of warrant rather than of qualification.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia before Islam remembered people who rejected the idols. They belonged to no community with a book. The word used here for upright attached to them in ordinary speech. So the audience had a living sense of what it named. Someone clearly devoted to one God, and clearly outside the settled religious groups of the region.
studies.didYouKnow: The word rendered upright appears twelve times in the Quran. Most of those uses describe Abraham. It is never used as the name of a community, unlike the two labels this ayah turns down. That is part of why it works here as an alternative to both of them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage makes a claim about what gives religious speech its warrant. Disagreement is not itself the fault. Disagreement without knowledge is. The passage then answers the original question by refusing both available labels. That suggests the categories communities sort themselves by may not reach back to the figures they are built on. What is offered instead describes which way he faced, not what he belonged to.

crossReferences.why: Answers the same claim by naming the upright way of Abraham, who associated nothing with God.
Calls him the one who named this community, carrying the description forward in time.
Describes a straight religion as the upright way of Abraham, spoken in the Prophet's own voice.

studies.applyIt: There is a specific discipline here: notice when you are arguing past the edge of what you actually know. Pick one topic you have opinions about and locate that edge honestly. Then, in the next conversation about it, say where the edge is, out loud. It is a small thing to say and unusually hard to do.
studies.explainEasier: God asks why people argue about things they do not know. Then He gives the answer plainly. Abraham was not a Jew and not a Christian. He simply turned away from false gods and gave himself to God.

studies.title: Nearest To Abraham
studies.meaning: Who has a claim on Abraham is answered by a test, not by a family line. Those closest to him are the ones who followed him. Then the prophet addressed here. Then those who believe. Early scholars note that descent is not mentioned at all. The ayah closes by naming God the guardian of the believers. That quietly replaces the whole frame of the dispute. What was being argued over was patronage, and the last clause assigns it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the short section that began with a question about arguing over Abraham. Claims of a link to famous ancestors carried real authority in the region. Communities in Medina traced themselves to him. Classical commentaries read this ayah as the answer to the argument set up two ayat earlier. It puts a test in place of an inherited claim, one anyone can meet or fail.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the root meaning to be close and to take charge. It covers proximity and the right that comes with it, so the ayah answers a question about entitlement and about closeness at once.
The verb of walking behind someone on a road. It names a relationship established by movement rather than by birth, which is precisely the shift this ayah is making.
From the same root as the comparative that opens the ayah. Ending on this word ties the two halves together: nearness to Abraham is answered by naming who is near to the believers.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Patronage was the structure of Arabian society. A client attached himself to a stronger party, and that bond determined who defended him, who spoke for him, and where he stood in any gathering. Claiming a great ancestor was a way of claiming a patron who could never withdraw the arrangement. The last clause of this ayah addresses exactly the need that made such claims valuable.
studies.didYouKnow: The comparative that opens this ayah and the noun that closes it come from the same root. So the argument and its answer are built out of one word. Turns of this kind, where a passage rests on one root in different forms, are a known feature of Quranic style. They are mostly invisible in translation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Belonging is redefined as following rather than descending. That makes a figure from history open to anyone and inheritable by no one. The effect reaches past the dispute at hand. It removes any claim on God's favour held by right of birth. The closing clause completes the move. It names the relationship believers actually have, and that is a gift rather than a claim.

crossReferences.why: Says the covenant with Abraham does not reach the wrongdoers among his own descendants.
Applies the same connection to the community addressed, calling it the way of Abraham.
Names God the guardian of those who believe, bringing them out of darkness into light.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you are counting on that you did not earn: a family reputation, a school, a community you were born into. None of it is bad to have. But this ayah puts following where inheritance was, so pick one thing you have inherited and identify the actual practice underneath it. Then do that practice this week.
studies.explainEasier: People argued about who Abraham really belonged to. God says the closest to him are the ones who followed him. That means this prophet and the people who believe. God looks after those who believe.

studies.title: They Only Mislead Themselves
studies.meaning: A wish is described, and then its effect is turned around. Some among the People of the Book would like to lead the believers astray. What happens is that they lead themselves astray instead. The last clause is the sharpest part: they do not perceive it. Early scholars note the careful limit to a party rather than a whole community. The surah keeps to that limit and returns to it openly a few ayat later.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section that addresses the scriptural communities of the city directly. The surah is careful with its scope. It speaks of a group among them here, and describes an upright group among them a few ayat later in warm terms. Classical commentaries keep that distinction. No particular occasion is reported for this ayah. The sources read it as a pattern rather than one episode.

keyTerms.note: A verb of affectionate wanting rather than of plotting. It names an inclination of the heart, which is why the ayah can describe an intention without reporting that anything was done.
A word for a portion of a larger body, from a root meaning to go around. Its use here is a deliberate limitation of scope, and the surah keeps to that limitation consistently.
From the root behind the words for a poet and for fine awareness. It names subtle noticing, so the denial says the harm is not merely unadmitted but genuinely unfelt by them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A guide who misled a caravan in the desert did not walk a separate road home. He was on the same route, out of water at the same hour, and the consequences of his direction reached him first. Everyone who had travelled understood that misdirection is not something you do to other people from a safe distance. The image behind this ayah was a practical fact of the trade routes.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a party used here recurs through this surah, and not only of others. It later names two groups among the believers who almost lost heart before a battle, and a group at Uhud preoccupied with their own concerns. The surah applies the same limiting term in both directions, which stops it becoming a label for one side.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah describes how a moral thing works. An attempt to damage someone else lands first on the one attempting it, and lands unseen. The first consequence of an intention sits inside the person who holds it. It arrives before anything at all reaches the target. The closing clause about not perceiving is what makes this serious. A harm you cannot feel is one you have no reason to stop.

crossReferences.why: Describes an upright group among the same community, reciting through the night and prostrating.
Uses the same reversal: they deceive only themselves, and they do not perceive it.
States the principle generally: an evil scheme encircles only the people who devise it.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you wanted something to go badly for someone. Not acted on it, only wanted it. Notice what that wanting did to you while you carried it, and how little it did to them. The claim in this ayah is not moral advice; it is a description of where the damage actually goes.
studies.explainEasier: Some people from the earlier faiths would like to pull the believers off the right road. But they only pull themselves off it. And they cannot even tell that this is happening to them.

studies.title: Truth Dressed In Falsehood
studies.meaning: Two questions are put in the same form, and both turn on one phrase: while you know. The first asks why signs are refused by people who are themselves witnesses to them. The second names two distinct acts, mixing truth with falsehood and concealing truth, and again attaches knowledge to both. Classical commentators observe that neither question asks whether the thing happened. The form assumes it and asks for a reason, which leaves the answer with the hearer.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, part of the surah's direct address to the scriptural communities of the city. Classical commentaries link the passage to disagreements in Medina about what the earlier scriptures held. They do not fix it to one episode. In this section the surah addresses a party, never everyone. It says so plainly a few ayat earlier and comes back to it later.

keyTerms.note: The verb literally means to dress something in a garment. Mixing truth with falsehood is pictured as putting the wrong clothes on a thing, so it is still there and no longer recognisable.
From a root for holding something back within, used of suppressing knowledge, evidence or grief. It names withholding what one has rather than asserting what is false.
The verb covers seeing something firsthand and testifying to it. Its use sharpens the first question, since a witness who denies is doing something different from a stranger who disbelieves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony held a society together where almost nothing was written down. In a dispute over a debt, a sale or a killing, a witness was the whole evidence. A man known to have hidden what he saw lost his standing for good. Everyone knew the difference between lying outright and simply not saying what you knew. The second was harder to prove and did just as much damage.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of clothing truth in falsehood appears more than once in the Quran. The verb belongs to the ordinary vocabulary of dress. Arabic uses one root for a garment and for confusion. That lets the text describe a subtle twisting with a completely everyday word rather than a technical one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names concealing as a wrong in its own right, apart from denial. Something can be kept accurately, held in full knowledge, and still be withheld at the moment it would count. Both questions say that those addressed know. So the failure named is one of will, not of understanding. That is where this surah has already placed division among people who share a text.

crossReferences.why: Names the same two acts together: do not clothe truth with falsehood, nor conceal it knowingly.
Traces division among scriptural communities to rivalry arising after knowledge had come.
Speaks of those who conceal what was sent down of clear proofs and of guidance.

studies.applyIt: Concealing is easier than lying and feels almost innocent. Think of one thing you know that would help someone if you said it, and that you have not said because saying it would cost you. You do not have to act today. Name the cost accurately to yourself first, because that is usually where the honesty is missing.
studies.explainEasier: God asks the people of earlier books two things. They turn away from His signs even though they can see them. They also mix the truth with lies and hide it, and they know they are doing it.

studies.title: Believe At Dawn, Refuse By Evening
studies.meaning: A tactic is quoted rather than described. Believe in the morning and reject by evening, the speakers say, so that the believers will turn back. The reasoning behind it is social. People known to have studied the scriptures reverse themselves in public. Others then conclude there was something in it worth reversing. Early scholars note that the passage exposes a plan simply by reporting it. The surah uses that method more than once in this section.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of the city. Classical commentaries report the tactic as concerning the change in the direction of prayer. They differ over the details. The surah puts it down to a group, not to everyone. The wording of the plan suggests a proposal made among a few people, not a position taken in public.

keyTerms.note: An idiom for its first part, the way a face is the front of a person. Arabic gives the day a face and an end, so the tactic is described in the vocabulary of a body turning.
The counterpart to the opening phrase, closing the figure. The pairing marks out a single day, which is what makes the reversal conspicuous rather than gradual and unremarkable.
The verb for going back the way you came. It names the intended effect on others: not a refutation of anything, but a retracing of steps that had already been taken.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Changing religion in a tribal society was public and it changed structures. It moved a person's alliances. It altered who would defend them. It was noticed at once by everyone who mattered. Nobody changed religion in private. That is what makes the tactic here believable. A visible reversal inside one day would have been talked about across the whole city before nightfall.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah quotes a plan directly, in the words of those making it. The Quran does that in several places with the schemes of opponents. Early scholars note that reporting a private proposal in public was itself a kind of answer. The tactic depended entirely on nobody knowing it was a tactic.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage assumes that conviction spreads both ways. People take their bearings partly from what others do. That is a realistic account of how belief moves, and the passage does not condemn it. What it exposes is the deliberate use of it as a lever. The tactic also depends on religious commitment being visible. The surah elsewhere treats that visibility as a strength rather than a weakness.

crossReferences.why: Describes wavering between two sides and belonging fully to neither, in similar terms.
Portrays those who profess belief without holding it, and the sickness in their hearts.
Continues the quoted speech, adding the instruction to trust only those of your own religion.

studies.applyIt: You are more influenced by other people's confidence than you think, and so is everyone around you. Pick one commitment you have quietly softened because somebody you respect seemed unimpressed by it. Reconsider it on its own terms this week, without reference to them. The tactic in this ayah only works on people who have never done that.
studies.explainEasier: Some people made a plan. They would say they believed the new message in the morning, then say they did not believe it by evening. They hoped that would make the believers doubt and go back.

studies.title: Guidance Is God's Guidance
studies.meaning: The quoted advice continues and narrows: trust only those who follow your own religion. The reply comes in two parts, each introduced by an instruction to speak. The first states that guidance belongs to God, so it is not a possession any community controls. The second names bounty as lying in God's hand, given to whom He wills. Classical commentators discuss the middle clause at length, since its structure allows more than one reading of who is speaking and where the quotation ends.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, carrying on the address begun in the ayah before. The worry being answered is a real one for any community with a long tradition. What it holds might also be given somewhere else. Classical commentaries read the passage as meeting that worry directly rather than brushing it aside. That is why the answer is about God's freedom to give, not about anyone being unworthy.

keyTerms.note: Carrying the definite article, so it names guidance as one single thing rather than a quality anyone might possess. Attaching it to God removes it from the inventory of what a community can hold in trust.
From a root meaning what remains over and above, an excess. It names a gift beyond anything owed, which is why it cannot be claimed as a right by any party at all.
An active participle from the verb to be wide. It describes God as having room, which in this context means that giving to one party does not reduce what remains available to another.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wells, grazing and trade routes were limited. Most goods were genuinely rival. What one tribe used, another could not. Standing worked the same way. Precedence was a fixed amount, split among a limited number of claimants. Describing God as vast pushes straight against that instinct. The audience would have felt how strange it was.
studies.didYouKnow: The name describing God as vast closes this ayah. It occurs several times in the Quran and is usually paired with knowledge, as it is here. Early scholars explain the pairing as a guard. Plenty does not mean giving without care. The giving is unlimited in reach and exact in where it lands.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage answers a question about who is inside by moving the thing being fought over. Guidance and bounty are not shares in a limited stock. They are gifts from a giver with no limit. So another community receiving something takes nothing from anyone else. That removes the logic behind religious rivalry. It does not deny that revelation is truly given to particular people at particular times.

crossReferences.why: Says God singles out for His mercy whom He wills, answering a comparable reluctance.
States plainly that guiding people is not the messenger's to do, but God's alone.
Completes the thought immediately: He singles out His mercy for whomever He wills.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether you feel a small drop when someone outside your circle does well at something you care about. That reaction assumes a fixed supply. The description at the end of this ayah says there is room. Test it once this week: when the feeling arrives, say the person's name and one true good thing about what they did.
studies.explainEasier: Some people said to trust only those who follow your own religion. God answers that guidance comes from Him. Good things are in His hand. He gives them to whoever He wants, and He has plenty to give.

studies.title: Singled Out For Mercy
studies.meaning: One short sentence completes the answer begun in the ayah before. It then closes on a description of God. Mercy is assigned specifically, to whom God wills. The verb means to set something apart for one particular receiver. Early scholars note that the passage never says why a given person is chosen. The argument around it does not need that. What it shows is where the decision sits, and that is enough to settle the dispute it belongs to.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the section that answers a worry about revelation being given to others. The two ayat work as a pair. One says bounty is in God's hand. This one says it is placed deliberately. Classical commentaries treat the pairing as the surah's answer to a long argument about which community holds what. They note that neither side is given a test to apply.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to set apart for a particular case, the opposite of what is general. It describes a gift addressed to someone in particular rather than distributed at large.
From the root that also gives Arabic its word for a womb. The Quran uses this term for guidance, revelation and rain alike, so what is being assigned here is deliberately left broad.
An adjective from a root connected to bone, so the sense is of something with substance and mass rather than merely large. It describes the bounty as having weight, not only extent.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Gifts in Arabia were public and specific. A chief distributed at a gathering and everyone saw who received what, so a gift was as much a statement about a relationship as a transfer of goods. Being singled out mattered more than the value of the object itself. The verb used here belongs to that world, where the act of assigning was the significant part.
studies.didYouKnow: The two ayat that close this section end on three descriptions of God in quick succession. Vast, knowing, and holder of immense bounty. Closing a passage with God's names is a structural habit of the Quran. Early scholars read the particular names chosen as a summary of the argument just made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Mercy is presented as specific, not merely general, and that changes what it is. A mercy reaching everyone equally would be a feature of the world. A mercy assigned on purpose is an act, and acts have an actor with intentions. The passage never explains those intentions. So the one who receives is left holding thanks, not an account of why they deserved it.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same verb of God singling out His mercy for whomever He wills.
Sets up this conclusion by placing all bounty in God's hand, given to whom He wills.
Tells the People of the Book that bounty is in God's hand, given out as He wills.

studies.applyIt: Think of one thing in your life you did nothing to arrange: where you were born, a person who took an interest in you early, a capacity you simply have. Name it specifically rather than in general. The verb here means singled out, and the practice it suggests is identifying what was addressed to you.
studies.explainEasier: God picks out who will receive His mercy. He gives it to whoever He wants. The good He hands out is very great. That choice is His alone to make.

studies.title: A Heap Of Gold, A Single Coin
studies.meaning: Two kinds of person are described inside the same community, and the description is carefully even. One will return a fortune left in his keeping. Another will not return a single coin unless you stand over him. The ayah then names the belief that made the second feel allowed. No debt is owed to outsiders. What is condemned is less the failure to repay than the rule invented to permit it. That rule, the ayah says, is put on God knowingly.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of the city. Trust in business between communities was ordinary in Medina. Deposits, loans and goods moved between people who did not share a religion. Classical commentaries treat the passage as describing a real pattern of conduct. They also hold to the distinction the ayah draws, since it names the trustworthy first.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives Arabic its words for faith, for safety and for a deposit left in trust. To entrust someone is to make yourself safe with them, which is why the same root covers belief.
The same word used earlier in this surah of heaped-up wealth. Its exact quantity was disputed by the early Arabic dictionary writers, but its sense of an enormous and unspecified sum never was.
The participle for standing, used of remaining insistently present. It pictures a creditor who has to physically stay there until he is paid, which is what recovery looked like without courts.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina had no bank and no bailiff. A traveller leaving for a season handed his savings to someone he judged reliable. The whole system rested on reputation. A man known to return deposits drew business. A man who did not was avoided, but could rarely be forced. Standing over a debtor until he paid was a shabby necessity everyone had either done or watched.
studies.didYouKnow: The two amounts named in this ayah cannot be compared. An unmeasured heap of gold is set against one named coin. Classical writers on style describe this as a device. The extremes are given so that the middle is understood. The word for the larger sum appears earlier in this surah, in a quite different argument.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates conduct from community. The trustworthy and the untrustworthy are placed inside the same group. The ayah will not let either stand for the whole. Its sharper claim is about the rule itself. Limiting honesty to your own people is called a lie put on God. That makes the error in belief come first, and the error in conduct follow from it.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same refusal to generalise, describing an upright group inside the same community.
States the general principle: render trusts back to the people they belong to.
Describes a deposit given without a written record, and calls for the trust to be discharged.

studies.applyIt: Notice whether your standard of honesty shifts with the person in front of you: a stranger, a large company, someone from outside your circle. It probably does, a little, and the shift usually arrives with a reason attached to it. Pick one such case this week and hold yourself to the standard you would use with a friend.
studies.explainEasier: Some people of the earlier books will give back a whole pile of gold you left with them. Others will not give back one coin unless you keep asking. They think they owe nothing to outsiders.

studies.theme: The Love Between God and the Believer
studies.title: God Loves The Mindful
studies.meaning: A single word opens the ayah and overturns what came before it. On the contrary: a debt is owed. The correction is then put positively, not as a rebuke. Whoever keeps his commitment and guards himself is loved by God. Early scholars note the shift from one case to a general rule, and from a named group to anyone at all. A claim about who deserves honesty is answered by a description open to everybody.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, answering the claim quoted in the ayah before, that no debt is owed to outsiders. The surah's method here is typical. A specific claim is met with a general rule, not with a counter-charge. Classical commentaries note that the reply names no community at all. That is what makes it a correction of the rule rather than of the people who held it.

keyTerms.note: A particle used only to contradict a negative statement, so it cannot be rendered by a simple yes. Its entire function is to overturn a denial that has just been made aloud.
From the root for completeness, used of paying a debt in full. Keeping a commitment is described as paying it out entirely, with nothing quietly withheld at the edges of it.
From a root meaning to take shelter behind something. It names people who move carefully because they are aware of what they are avoiding, rather than people who have achieved a rank.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A promise in Arabia was enforced by nothing but reputation and kin. There was no registry and no contract law. No authority could compel a man across a tribal boundary. What held the system together was simple. A person's word was the whole of their credit, and everyone knew whose word was good. A promise kept was the currency the economy ran on.
studies.didYouKnow: This surah states what God loves and does not love more often than most chapters of the Quran. The statements are spread across its whole length rather than gathered in one place. The pattern gives the surah a running commentary on character. That runs alongside its arguments about belief and history.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God's love is attached here to a condition anyone can meet. The condition is a kept promise, not a membership or a rite. That places ordinary reliability among the things that matter most. The wording matters too. The ayah does not say God loves the one who did this. It names a whole class. So the love is described as a settled leaning rather than a reaction.

crossReferences.why: Quotes the claim this ayah overturns, that no obligation is owed to outsiders.
Opens a whole surah with the instruction to fulfil commitments, before anything else is said.
Says a commitment will be asked about, treating the promise itself as something accountable.

studies.applyIt: Think of a small promise you made recently and have quietly let slide, the kind nobody would chase you for. Do it today, badly if necessary, rather than well next month. The word in this ayah means paid in full, and small unpaid promises are the ones that decide what people can actually rely on you for.
studies.explainEasier: God says that keeping your word does matter. Whoever keeps a promise and stays careful about right and wrong is loved by God. It does not depend on which group a person belongs to.

studies.title: Sold For A Small Price
studies.meaning: The transaction is described as a sale, and all its force lies in the price. What is handed over is a covenant with God and a person's own sworn word. What is received is called small, and never named. Four consequences follow. Three of them are withdrawals rather than punishments: no speech, no look, no declaring clean. Early scholars note that the punishment itself comes last and briefly. It reads as though the loss of regard were the heavier part.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the discussion of trusts and commitments. Classical commentaries report several occasions for this ayah. They involve false oaths sworn to secure property or to win a dispute, and the reports differ in their details. So the sources treat it as a general statement about oaths taken lightly. It arose where a sworn word settled cases that no evidence could.

keyTerms.note: The verb of purchase, used in the Quran for trading one thing away for another. Describing this as a purchase makes the person an active party who looked at the terms and accepted them.
Deliberately left unquantified. Early scholars note that any price would be small against what is given up, so the adjective describes the exchange itself rather than the sum received.

An older word for a lot assigned to someone, related to the root for creating and apportioning. It names not a reward but the share a person would otherwise have had, which is why its absence reads as loss.
From a root covering growth and purification together. It carries the sense of pronouncing someone clean as well as making them so, so the denial withholds vindication as much as cleansing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An oath sworn before witnesses closed a case. Where there was no document and no outside testimony, a solemn oath was the last instrument. Communities accepted it because the alternative was violence. A man who swore falsely gained the disputed property outright. The system worked only because most people believed a false oath cost more than the goods.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the three withdrawals named here appear together again in Surah 2. They are that God will not speak to them and will not declare them clean. That passage is about concealing revelation for a price. The Quran repeats such clusters of denials. Adding the third element makes this the fullest form of the formula.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The consequences described are about relationship rather than penalty. Not being spoken to, not being looked at, not being declared clean: each is a removal of regard. All three are listed before any mention of suffering. That suggests a loss centred on a relationship ending, not on pain. It puts the weight somewhere other than where fear usually assumes it lies.

crossReferences.why: Names the same withdrawals, of those who conceal what was revealed in exchange for a price.
Warns against using oaths as an instrument of deceit, and calls the price a little thing.
States the positive form immediately before: God loves the one who fulfils his commitment.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you have actually traded your word for recently. Usually it is not money. It is convenience, or avoiding an awkward conversation, or looking better than you are. Name the price out loud, in its real currency. The argument here is entirely about the exchange rate, and most people have never checked theirs.
studies.explainEasier: Some people trade away their promise to God and their own sworn word for a small gain. They will have no share in the life to come. God will not speak to them or look at them.

studies.title: Twisting With The Tongue
studies.meaning: A group is described who bend their tongues while reciting. What they say then sounds like scripture and is taken for it. The ayah repeats itself on purpose. It is not from the Book. It is not from God. Early scholars discuss what the twisting involved, whether a change in delivery, in wording, or in the sense conveyed, and they keep the whole range. What nobody disputes is how it works. It rests on the authority of a voice, not on the content of any claim.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of Medina. Reciting the earlier scriptures there was a public and respected act. Classical commentaries link the passage to disputes about what those scriptures actually held. They read the ayah as describing a practice rather than one occasion. The Quran limits it to a party, as it does throughout this section.

keyTerms.note: The verb for turning something out of its straight line, used of twisting a rope or turning the head aside. Applied to tongues it makes the distortion physical rather than merely intellectual.
The plural of the organ, which in Arabic also means a language. Locating the fault in the tongue rather than in a text places it in the act of delivery, where a listener cannot inspect it.
A verb of calculation and supposition, from the root for counting. It names an estimate made under limited information, which is exactly the position of anyone listening to a recitation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scripture in that world was heard far more often than it was read. Few could check a text, copies were rare and expensive, and authority belonged to the person reciting. A trained voice carried its own credibility, and an audience listening to a language it did not fully command had no way of testing what it heard. The vulnerability this ayah describes was structural.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for twisting appears elsewhere in the Quran of people turning their heads away. The same root gives Arabic its word for a bend in a road. The image stays the same across those uses. Something that ought to run straight is being pushed aside without ever being broken.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names a kind of dishonesty that leaves every single statement intact. Nothing is denied and nothing is openly invented. The false impression comes from the manner of delivery alone. Calling this a lie about God, rather than about a text, sets a high standard for religious speech. What a speaker answers for is the impression created, not only the words used.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same twisting of tongues, adding that it is a slandering of the religion.
Speaks of writing a book with one's own hands and saying it is from God, for a small price.
Names the parallel act a few ayat earlier: clothing truth in falsehood and concealing it.

studies.applyIt: Notice the difference between saying something false and building a false impression out of true things. The second is far more common and much easier to excuse. Pick one situation this week where you were accurate on the surface and misleading on purpose. Then correct the impression rather than the words.
studies.explainEasier: Some people twist their words while reading out loud. They make it sound like it comes from the holy book when it does not. They say it is from God when it is not, and they know.

studies.title: No One Given Scripture Would Say
studies.meaning: The claim is about what a prophet could not do. Someone given a book, sound judgement and prophecy would never turn round and ask people to worship him. The ayah then supplies what such a person would say instead. It uses a rare word for those who belong wholly to the Lord. It roots that condition in two ordinary activities: teaching scripture and studying it. Early scholars note that the alternative offered is a practice, not a rank.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, part of the surah's dealings with the Christian community of Najran. It also meets wider disputes about the standing of prophets and teachers. Classical commentaries report that the ayah answers a question. The question was whether obedience of the kind owed to God might be given to a prophet. The surah's answer speaks about prophets in general, not about any single figure, as the whole section does.

keyTerms.note: From the root for making firm and for issuing a ruling. Named separately from the Book, it points to the capacity to apply what is known, which possession of a text does not by itself supply.

A rare word built directly on the word for Lord. The early Arabic dictionary writers connect it with deep learning joined to devotion, and describe it as naming teachers whose knowledge is turned toward God.
From a root meaning to efface by repeated passing over, as a road is worn into a track. Study in Arabic is wearing something smooth by returning to it, not acquiring it once and moving on.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Teachers in the ancient world held real power over their students. Religious authority in the region ran through scholars who could read what most people could only hear. A teacher's word settled matters of practice for a whole community. The pull this ayah describes was not imagined. The audience knew of households whose loyalties followed one learned man.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for those wholly given to the Lord occurs only three times in the Quran. It appears once here and twice in a later surah. Each time it names learned teachers among earlier communities. It is among the rarest terms the Quran uses for a kind of religious person, and it has no plural counterpart elsewhere.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a limit on religious authority from inside the office, not from outside it. The very gifts that make someone worth following are what make a demand for worship impossible. The passage also moves the goal of teaching. Those taught are to become people of the Lord themselves. So teaching aims at standing on your own before God, not at leaning on a teacher.

crossReferences.why: Continues the same argument: nor would he tell you to take angels and prophets as lords.
Shows Jesus questioned about exactly this, and disowning it in the plainest possible terms.
Describes a community taking its scholars and monks as lords apart from God.

studies.applyIt: If you learn from someone, a teacher, a speaker, an author, notice whether their effect is to send you toward the source or to keep you coming back to them. Both patterns are common. Test it this week by acting on one thing you learned from them without checking back in with them first.
studies.explainEasier: No one God gave a book and prophethood would tell people to worship him. He would tell them to belong to God instead. That is what teaching the book and studying it is for.

studies.title: Angels And Prophets Are Not Lords
studies.meaning: The argument continues into its second half. The same person who could not ask to be worshipped could not tell others to take angels or prophets as lords. So the ban reaches past his own case to every go-between. Then a question closes it: would he order refusal after you have submitted. Early scholars note that the question does the work an argument would otherwise have to do. The oddity is meant to be felt, not proved.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the ayah before it as one argument. Reverence for angels and for prophets was present in several religious communities of the region. The surah does not list the forms it took. Classical commentaries treat the ayah as addressing the general principle, not any one practice. That fits the way this whole section speaks of prophets in the plural.

keyTerms.note: The plural of the word used throughout the Quran for God as Lord. Its root covers ownership, nurture and authority together, so taking someone as a lord means placing your affairs under them.
A verb of adopting or acquiring something for one's own use. It implies an act by the person doing it, rather than a status the other party has claimed or asked for.
From a root meaning to cover or bury, used of a farmer covering seed with soil. Refusal in Arabic is pictured as covering something already present rather than as failing to notice it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia before Islam treated go-betweens as a normal part of religion. Gods were approached through lesser figures. Some traditions held that certain beings were partners of the high god, an arrangement the Quran addresses elsewhere. The audience grasped the appeal of a go-between at once. They had only recently left a system built around one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for lord appears here in the plural, which is unusual. The Quran normally uses it of God alone, in the singular. The plural form occurs only a handful of times in the whole Book. Each time it sits inside an argument about go-betweens. So the number of the word is itself part of the point.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage closes a route that religious history keeps reopening. Honour paid to a genuinely honourable figure slowly turns into something else. What is notable is the way the passage closes it. It does not lower angels or prophets at all. Their standing is left fully intact, and only the direction of worship is fixed. That split between honour and worship is what the section rests on.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same plural word for lords in the invitation to a common word between communities.
Describes a comparable arrangement, taking scholars and monks as lords apart from God.
Answers a similar argument, insisting Jesus was a servant on whom favour was bestowed.

studies.applyIt: Notice who you go to first when something goes wrong. Not who you believe in, but who you actually contact. There is nothing wrong with having people you trust, and this ayah diminishes nobody. It simply asks you to know the order, and the order is visible in what you reach for first.
studies.explainEasier: A true prophet would never tell people to treat angels as their masters. He would not say that about other prophets either. He would not ask people to turn away from God after they had given themselves to God.

studies.title: The Covenant Of The Prophets
studies.meaning: A covenant is reported, taken from the prophets themselves rather than from their communities. Its terms are conditional. You have been given scripture and wisdom. If a messenger comes confirming what you hold, you will believe in him and support him. Scholars differ over whether the pledge binds the prophets in person or their communities through them. The classical commentaries record both readings. The scene closes with an affirmation, a call to bear witness, and God naming Himself among the witnesses.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the argument that began with what a prophet could and could not say. The passage addresses a live question in Medina. Was accepting a later messenger a break with an earlier covenant, or one of its own terms. Classical commentaries read this as the surah's answer. It places support for a confirming messenger inside the original agreement, not in competition with it.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to tie firmly, related to a trusted bond and to a knot. It names an agreement made secure, and is stronger than the ordinary Arabic word for a promise.
A word for a heavy load or a tie that holds something down. It names an obligation by its weight, and the Quran uses it elsewhere of burdens people ask to be relieved of.
From a root meaning to settle and come to rest. Affirming in Arabic is letting a matter settle into place, so the question asks whether the terms have been accepted as final.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Covenants in Arabia were sealed in public, and the witnesses present were the whole of the enforcement. Two parties spoke the terms aloud. Those standing by were expected to remember, and to testify if a dispute arose later. A covenant without witnesses was nearly worthless. The scene here follows that shape exactly, down to the call for the parties to bear witness themselves.
studies.didYouKnow: God naming Himself among the witnesses to His own covenant is a striking turn. A witness is normally a third party to an agreement. Early scholars discuss it as a way of making the covenant heavier. This surah uses the language of witnessing again and again, including in the disciples' prayer to be written among the witnesses.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage frames the line of prophets as a matter of agreement, not of replacement. Each prophet is described as having accepted a duty in advance. He would support a later messenger who confirms what he holds. That makes the carrying over a term of the original covenant. So recognising a later revelation is faithfulness to the earlier one, not a break with it.

crossReferences.why: Recalls a covenant taken from the prophets, naming several of them individually.
Describes a covenant taken from those given the Book, to make it clear and not conceal it.
Speaks of a messenger found described in what earlier communities already held.

studies.applyIt: Think about a commitment you made in advance, before you knew what it would require: a marriage, a job, a friendship, a faith. Covenants of that shape are agreed under one set of conditions and tested under another. Name the one you are currently inside, and what it is actually asking of you now.
studies.explainEasier: God made a deal with the prophets. Each one was given a book and wisdom. If a later messenger came and agreed with what they had, they would believe him and help him. They all said yes.

studies.title: Willingly Or Unwillingly
studies.meaning: Two short ayat close the argument. The first names what follows from turning away after affirming. The second widens the frame completely. It asks whether some religion other than God's is being sought. Everything in the heavens and the earth has already submitted to Him, willingly or not. Early scholars explain that phrase as covering two things at once. Creation submits because it must. Those who choose submit because they choose. The phrase holds both without folding one into the other.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the section on the covenant of the prophets. The question put here is general, not aimed at any named group. Classical commentaries read the pairing as a typical move of this surah. It goes from a specific dispute outward to a frame as wide as the universe. They note that the argument is drawn from creation rather than from scripture. So it stands on its own, apart from the debate before it.

keyTerms.note: From a root used of a date breaking out of its skin. It names stepping outside a boundary rather than denying that one exists, so it describes conduct after an agreement rather than before.
A pair of verbal nouns naming the two modes of compliance. Setting them together covers the whole range without saying which creatures fall where, which lets the phrase describe everything at once.
The same verb as the religion named earlier in this surah, applied here to the heavens and the earth. Using one word for creation's submission and a human being's is the passage's central move.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in that world visibly obeyed something. The stars turned on a schedule navigators trusted with their lives, the seasons arrived, the camel knelt when it was made to kneel. Human beings were the conspicuous exception, the one part of the arrangement that argued back. An audience living close to the physical world would have felt the contrast the question depends on.
studies.didYouKnow: The pair of words for willing and unwilling occurs four times in the Quran. Three of those describe the whole created order submitting or prostrating, and one describes human spending. The phrase is almost reserved for statements about creation as a whole, which is precisely how this ayah uses it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage roots a religious claim in what can be seen of the world, not in a text. That lets it speak to anyone at all. If everything else already submits, the human question is not whether to submit. It is whether to do it knowingly. That difference, between going along and agreeing, is where the passage puts the whole weight of human choice.

crossReferences.why: Says everything in the heavens and earth prostrates to God, willingly or unwillingly.
Reports the heavens and the earth answering that they come willingly when summoned.
Supplies the covenant that turning away, in the first of these two ayat, refers back to.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your day you already spend complying with things you never chose: gravity, tiredness, the need to eat, other people's schedules. The question here is not whether you will submit to anything. It is which of your compliances you have ever actually agreed to. Pick one and agree to it deliberately today.
studies.explainEasier: Whoever turns away after that is going outside the line. Everything in the sky and on the earth already gives itself up to God, whether it wants to or not. And everything goes back to Him.

studies.title: We Make No Distinction
studies.meaning: A statement of belief is given as a list, and the list is deliberately long. What was revealed here. What was given to Abraham and his line. What Moses and Jesus and the prophets received. Then comes the clause that carries the weight. No distinction is made between any of them. Early scholars read this as a refusal to pick and choose, taking one messenger and turning down another. They do not read it as a claim that all prophets stand at the same rank.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the covenant of the prophets and what came of it. The declaration is placed in the community's own mouth. It answers a dispute about which revelations count. Classical commentaries note that a nearly identical statement appears in an earlier surah. They read the repeat here as its use in the arguments this chapter has been running.

keyTerms.note: A word for the lines descending from Jacob's sons, from a root associated with extension. It names a lineage collectively rather than any individual, which keeps the list from becoming a roll of names.
An intensive verb for dividing a thing into parts. Denying it means refusing to sort the messengers into accepted and rejected, which is exactly the practice the ayah is answering.
The participle from the root this surah uses for the religion God accepts. Placing it at the very end turns the whole preceding list into an account of what that submission consists of.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Alliances in Arabia were held or broken one clan at a time. A party could be at peace with one branch of a tribe and at war with another. Picking and choosing was the ordinary shape of politics. The refusal to separate, stated here about messengers, ran against a habit of mind. The audience applied that habit to nearly every relationship they had.
studies.didYouKnow: A nearly identical declaration appears twice in Surah 2. The wording differs slightly, and so does who is speaking. Comparing the three versions is a standard exercise in the commentaries. The small changes show one creed placed in different mouths and put to work in different arguments.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage defines faith partly by what it refuses to do. Accepting some messengers and rejecting others is one error, whichever ones are chosen. It makes the believer the one doing the choosing. The list also takes in figures other communities claim as their own. That turns a creed into a statement of overlap rather than of difference.

crossReferences.why: Gives almost the same declaration, with the same list and the same refusal to distinguish.
Describes those who believe in some messengers and disbelieve in others, and names it plainly.
Places the same words in the mouths of the believers, adding that they hear and obey.

studies.applyIt: Read the list slowly and notice how many of these names belong to communities you may think of as other. The creed you hold already contains them. If you have ever spoken about those communities as though they had nothing to do with you, read this ayah twice before the next such conversation.
studies.explainEasier: The believers say what they believe. They believe in God and in what was sent to them. They also believe in what was given to Abraham, Moses, Jesus and the other prophets. They accept all of them.

studies.title: What Will Not Be Accepted
studies.meaning: The word translated Islam is the verbal noun for surrender to God. The ayah says that anything else sought as a religion will not be accepted. Early scholars read the term alongside the surah's earlier definition and the list of prophets just given. On that reading it names the stance every prophet taught. It does not name a community set apart from them. The verb for seeking matters too. It describes a person going after something, not one who never met it.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, right after the declaration of belief in every messenger. The order matters, and classical commentaries note it. The creed naming Abraham, Moses and Jesus comes first. This ayah follows from it, so the two are read together. The surah has already defined the term in question earlier, in a passage about division arising after knowledge came.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form of the verb to seek, describing deliberate pursuit. It names someone actively going after an alternative rather than someone who has simply not been reached by anything.
The verbal noun from the root for handing something over whole. This surah has already used it for what every prophet brought, and that is the sense the commentators carry into this ayah.
From the vocabulary of trade, naming a merchant whose venture returns less than it cost him. It describes the outcome of a transaction rather than a penalty imposed from outside.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade was how Arabians understood risk. A merchant put money into a caravan. He either came back with a profit or came back short. The word for that shortfall was ordinary trading language. Calling the outcome of a life a loss was not an insult. It was an accounting word, and it landed on people who had watched ventures fail.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for religion and the word used for surrender both appear earlier in this surah. They come together in a single ayah that sets out how they relate. The two passages sit more than sixty ayat apart. The second assumes the definition given in the first. That is one of the ways this surah builds an argument across its whole length.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The force of the ayah depends on what its central term means. The surah has taken care to define that term before using it here. Understood as surrender to God, the claim is not that a label is required. It is that a stance is required. The list of prophets just given shows that stance running through every revelation. So the statement stays demanding without becoming a question of membership.

crossReferences.why: Defines the same term earlier in this surah, as the religion accepted with God.
Supplies the creed immediately before, naming every prophet without distinction.
Describes whoever surrenders his face to God while doing good as having his reward.

studies.applyIt: The word at the centre of this ayah means handing something over whole. Pick one area of your life you have kept back, not out of defiance but because you never got round to it. Name it specifically. Then hand over the smallest decision inside it today, and notice what that actually feels like.
studies.explainEasier: God says that He will only accept one thing from a person. That is giving yourself over to Him. Anyone who looks for some other way will end up with nothing in the life to come.

studies.title: After They Had Believed
studies.meaning: A question is asked rather than a verdict handed down. The question is about guidance, not about punishment. How would God guide people who refused after belief, after testifying that the messenger is true, and after clear proofs reached them. Early scholars note that the ayah stacks three stages of knowledge before the refusal. What is described is not a mistake but a reversal. The closing clause makes it general and names the condition wrongdoing.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical commentaries report occasions involving people who left the community and later sought to return. The reports vary in their details and in whom they concern. Because they differ, the sources read the ayah as a general statement about reversal after knowledge. They give particular weight to the ayah a few lines later that opens a door back.

keyTerms.note: An interrogative of manner rather than of possibility. It asks by what route guidance could reach such a person, which leaves the answer open in a way that a flat denial would not.
From a root meaning to be distinct and separated out. The word names evidence that has already done its work of distinguishing, so it describes clarity achieved rather than merely offered.
From a root meaning darkness and, in usage, putting a thing where it does not belong. Wrongdoing in Arabic is misplacement, which is why one word covers injustice and associating others with God.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Turning back in a tribal society was ruinous, and therefore rare. Leaving a community meant leaving its protection. Returning meant facing everyone who had watched you go. People did it anyway, under pressure from family, from debt or from fear. The audience knew of particular cases. That is part of why the surah addresses the situation head on.
studies.didYouKnow: This passage runs to four ayat, and its severity is reversed in the last of them. That ayah opens with a single word meaning except. The shape is typical of the Quran. Long warnings are often closed by an exception clause. It names those who turn back and put matters right.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage places the difficulty in the person, not in God's willingness. Guidance is not described as withheld out of anger. It is described as having nothing left to work with. Everything guidance normally supplies has already been supplied and set aside. Calling the condition wrongdoing rather than error frames it as a matter of what was done with knowledge. It is not a matter of what was understood.

crossReferences.why: Reverses this passage three ayat later, excepting those who repent and set things right.
Describes repeated movement in and out of belief, and its effect on the possibility of guidance.
Distinguishes one compelled to speak against faith from one who opens his chest to refusal.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this is a question and not a sentence, and notice where the passage goes three ayat later, which is to an exception. If you are carrying something you believe has put you outside the door, read to the end of the passage before deciding. Most people stop at the severity and never reach the clause that follows.
studies.explainEasier: These people believed, then turned away. They had seen the messenger was telling the truth. They had seen clear proof. God asks how He could guide people who did that.

studies.title: Except Those Who Turn Back
studies.meaning: Three ayat move from the heaviest language in the section to its reversal. The first names a penalty: the rejection of God, the angels and all people. The second says it is not lightened and no reprieve is granted. The third begins with a single word meaning except. Everything before it is then qualified. Early scholars note that repentance alone is not what is named. It is paired with putting things right. So an inward turn is joined to a repair that can be seen.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about turning away after belief. Classical commentaries report that people in this situation did return. The exception clause was understood as applying to real cases, not as a formality. The sources treat the sequence as deliberate. The severity is stated fully first. That way the exception cannot be read as a softening of what was said.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to drive away and expel. The English word curse suggests an incantation; the Arabic describes a distancing, being put outside rather than being harmed by a formula.
A passive verb from the root for lightness of weight. It pictures the punishment as a load, so relief would mean a reduction in what is carried rather than a shortening of the time it lasts.
The verb for returning to a place you came from. Repentance in Arabic is a change of direction rather than an emotion, which is why the ayah can pair it with a visible action.
From the root for soundness and for reconciliation between people. It names mending what was damaged, and its inclusion here keeps the turning from being a purely inward event.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Being driven out was the harshest thing an Arabian community could do to a person. It removed protection entirely. A man could then be killed without consequence. That is why exile was kept for the gravest offences. Coming back was possible, but it took a public act of repair, usually a payment. The wording of these ayat maps closely onto that procedure.
studies.didYouKnow: The exception clause here is the third part of a three-ayah unit. The word it opens with is the shortest in the passage. Early scholars point out that the Quran often attaches such clauses to its severest statements. Their placement is consistent across those cases. It always comes after the warning has been completed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The structure carries the theology. The passage states the full weight of a consequence and then admits an exception. That keeps both seriousness and possibility intact. Either one on its own would distort the picture. Pairing the turn with repair says something more. The door back is open, and it opens onto work rather than onto a declaration.

crossReferences.why: Poses the question this passage answers, about guidance after knowledge was set aside.
States the widest form of the same promise, telling servants not to despair of God's mercy.
Joins repentance to righteous action, and describes evil deeds being exchanged for good.

studies.applyIt: If you have decided something is past mending, notice that this passage names two things rather than one. Turning back, and repairing. The second is usually the part that has actually been avoided. Pick the smallest piece of repair open to you, something plain and doable this week. Do that first.
studies.explainEasier: These people are shut out by God, by the angels, and by everyone. Their punishment will not be made lighter. But there is one way out. If they turn back and put things right, God forgives.

studies.title: Deeper Than A Single Turn
studies.meaning: The ayat before opened a door for those who turn back and repair. This one describes a case where the door is closed. The wording is precise: refusal after belief, and then an increase in refusal. Early scholars note that the second clause carries the weight. What is described is not one reversal but a settled and deepening direction. Several read the closing of repentance as belonging to the moment of death. At that point turning has become impossible rather than merely unwanted.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, right after the exception clause that admitted those who repent. The two ayat are read together in the commentaries, since one opens what the other appears to close. Classical sources link the passage to people who left the community and kept moving away from it. Reports differ over the particulars. So the commentaries treat the description as a general one.

keyTerms.note: A reflexive form of the verb to add, so the increase is something done to oneself. It describes accumulation over time rather than a single act, which is what separates this case from the previous ayah.
The noun from the verb for returning. Naming it as a possession, their turning, points at something offered rather than at an inward state, which is why commentators discuss when it is offered.
From a root used of a traveller losing the road and of a thing mislaid. It names being off the path rather than opposing it, which is a different image from defiance.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A traveller who took a wrong turn in the desert could correct it within an hour and be fine. The same wrong turn, continued for a day, carried him past the wells he knew and beyond the reach of his own memory of the route. Distance did the damage, not the original error. Every caravan traveller understood that a mistake grew costlier the longer you kept going.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah and the one before it sit side by side and pull in opposite directions. One admits repentance. The other describes it as not accepted. Early scholars treat the pairing as deliberate rather than a contradiction. A good deal of the commentary literature is about how the two are to be held together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates a single reversal from a direction. What is described as beyond acceptance is not one act. It is a course continued and added to. So the difficulty lies in built-up momentum, not in the severity of any single decision. Read beside the ayah before it, the two describe an open door. They also describe the chance of walking too far from it to turn.

crossReferences.why: Opens the door this ayah appears to close, for those who turn back and put things right.
Says repentance is not for those who persist until death arrives at the door.
Describes faith arriving too late to benefit, once the consequence is already visible.

studies.applyIt: The difference this ayah draws is between a mistake and a direction. Look at something you have been doing that you already know is wrong, and ask honestly whether you are still at the first stage or have been adding to it for a while. Then turn now rather than later, because the distinction here is about distance.
studies.explainEasier: Some people believed, then turned away, and then went further and further away. Their turning back will not be taken any more. They have wandered right off the road and lost their way.

studies.title: The Earth Full Of Gold
studies.meaning: The largest sum the language can build is named and then refused. Gold equal to the whole earth would not be taken as a ransom from someone who died refusing. Early scholars observe that the ayah does not call the gold worthless. It says the payment will not be taken. That is a statement about the deal, not about the metal. The closing clause repeats a formula used earlier in the surah about having nobody to help.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the sequence about turning away after belief. The passage speaks of a condition at the moment of death, not of any living person. Classical commentaries stress that point. The argument turns on how final the state is, not on how severe it is. No particular occasion is reported. The sources read it as a general statement following the discussion before it.

keyTerms.note: A construction naming the amount needed to fill something. Applied to the earth it produces the largest quantity ordinary Arabic can express, without naming any number at all.
From the root for redeeming a captive by payment, a familiar transaction across Arabia. It assumes a world in which almost anything could be settled for the right price.
Specified rather than left as wealth in general. Gold was the one commodity whose value held across borders and across generations, which is why it stands here for value itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Ransom was ordinary. Captives taken in raids were returned for payment, blood claims were settled in camels, and even a life could be priced. The system was practical rather than cynical, since it kept feuds from consuming whole tribes. In that world, being told a payment would not be accepted was stranger than being told the price was high, because it meant leaving the system altogether.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of the earth's fill of gold offered as ransom appears elsewhere in the Quran, with a variation. There, those who wronged would offer everything on earth and as much again alongside it. The figure comes back in several places. It always describes an exchange that cannot be made.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage marks the boundary of exchange. Almost everything in the audience's world could be settled by payment. The ayah names the largest payment imaginable to say that this matter is not of that kind. What is described is a difference in kind, not a shortfall in the amount. That is why the closing clause about helpers follows so naturally.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same image, everything on earth offered again over, and refused as ransom.
Denies that any ransom will be taken or intercession accepted on that day.
Ends with the identical phrase about having no helpers, earlier in this surah.

studies.applyIt: Notice how many of your problems you quietly solve with money or with something equivalent: time bought, tasks paid away, discomfort outsourced. That is not wrong and it works. Then name one thing in your life that is genuinely not of that kind. Most people can find one, and most people avoid looking at it.
studies.explainEasier: Some people refuse the truth and die still refusing. If one of them tried to pay with enough gold to fill the whole earth, it would not be taken. Nobody will come to help them.

studies.title: Until You Give What You Love
studies.meaning: Two distinct movements sit in this unit. The first sets a condition on goodness itself. You will not reach it until you spend from what you love. So the measure named is attachment, not amount. The second turns to an argument about food. Everything was permitted to the Children of Israel, except what Israel restricted for himself before the Torah came down. The ayah then invites the disputing party to bring the Torah and read it aloud.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical scholars report that companions of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) answered the first ayah at once. They gave away particular possessions they valued most. Reports of who gave what vary, while agreeing on the pattern. The second ayah belongs to the surah's discussion with the scriptural communities of Medina. The question was which food rules were the original ones, and the ayah challenges them to produce the text.

keyTerms.note: A word for wide-reaching good, from a root associated with open land. It covers devotion, kindness to parents and honest dealing at once, which is why the Quran uses it as a summary term.
The verb for laying out money, from a root also connected with a tunnel and with something running out. Spending in Arabic is described by depletion rather than by transfer to someone else.
The ordinary verb for love, used here of possessions. Its presence shifts the condition from a quantity to a relationship, since two people giving the same sum are not doing the same thing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Wealth in Medina was specific and named. A man did not own a portfolio; he owned a particular date grove, a particular well, a named horse. Everyone knew which property was whose, and which of a man's holdings he cared about most. Giving from what you loved was therefore a public and identifiable act, and the community could see exactly what had changed hands.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for goodness anchors a well-known passage in Surah 2. There, goodness is defined not as facing a direction in prayer but as a list of beliefs and practical acts. The two passages define one term from different angles. One does it by content, the other by cost.
