studies.theologicalSignificance: The condition set here makes giving a matter of what is inside the giver, not of what the receiver gains. A gift that costs nothing may still help someone. But it is described as not reaching the thing named. That puts attachment at the centre of the moral question. The closing clause says God knows whatever is spent. So the point extends to gifts nobody ever sees.

crossReferences.why: Defines the same word for goodness by a list of beliefs and acts rather than by direction.
Warns against giving away the poor part of what you have, which you would not take yourself.
Describes feeding others while loving the food, and wanting nothing back for it.

studies.applyIt: Look around the room you are in and find something you would rather not give away. That is this ayah's measure, and it has nothing to do with the price. You do not have to part with that object. But give something this week whose absence you would actually notice, and see whether it registers differently.
studies.explainEasier: You will not be truly good until you give away something you love. God knows whatever you give. All food was allowed for the Children of Israel. The only things left out were the ones Israel gave up himself.

studies.title: The First House For People
studies.meaning: Three ayat move from a warning to an instruction to a claim about a place. Anyone inventing about God after the challenge just issued is named a wrongdoer. Then the instruction is to follow the way of Abraham. He is described again as inclining to God and not among those who associate. Then the argument shifts ground entirely, to the first house set up for humanity. Early scholars read the third ayah as answering a question of precedence. It points to a building older than the dispute.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical commentaries link the passage to arguments in Medina about which sanctuary came first. The community had recently been told to face Mecca in prayer, so the question was live. The surah's answer is about dates rather than about scoring a point. That matches the argument it made earlier about the timing of the Torah and the Gospel next to Abraham himself.

keyTerms.note: A word for the whole practice a community follows, distinct from the word for religion used elsewhere in this surah. It names a road walked by a group rather than an allegiance owed to someone.
A name for the valley of the sanctuary, used only here in the Quran. Early scholars discuss its relation to the more familiar name and connect it with crowding and with people pressing together.
The passive of the verb to place. Using the passive leaves the builder unnamed at this point, which puts the weight on the house's priority in time rather than on who raised it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sanctuaries organised Arabian life. Trade fairs, truces and pilgrimage seasons gathered around them. The tribe that kept one drew income and standing from it. So claims about which sanctuary came first were about money as much as about religion. The audience heard a claim about the first house as a claim about where the centre of the peninsula really lay.
studies.didYouKnow: The name used for the sanctuary's valley in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The more familiar name appears exactly once, in a later surah. The early Arabic dictionary writers connect the form used here with a root meaning to crowd or press together. They relate that to how thickly people stand around the house.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage rests a claim on dates rather than on merit. That is the same move the surah made about Abraham and the later scriptures. What is asserted is being first in time and being for everyone in purpose. The house was set down for people, not for a tribe, and is called guidance for all beings. That framing makes the place a sign rather than a possession. The next ayah treats it that way.

crossReferences.why: Shows Abraham and his son raising the foundations of the same house, and praying over it.
Uses the same chronological argument earlier in this surah, about Abraham and the scriptures.
Describes the site of the house being appointed to Abraham, with instructions for its use.

studies.applyIt: The argument here rests on what came first. Try applying that to something you inherited without asking: a family habit, a way of marking a season, a phrase you use often. Find out where it actually started. Knowing the origin of a practice usually changes how tightly you hold the version you were handed.
studies.explainEasier: God says to follow the way of Abraham, who turned to God alone. The first house of worship ever built for people stands at Bekka. It is blessed, and it is a guide for everyone.

studies.title: Whoever Enters It Is Secure
studies.meaning: The house is described by what is in it and what happens there. There are clear signs, and one is named: the place where Abraham stood. Then comes a statement of security. Early scholars read that in two ways at once. It covers the historical safety of the sanctuary and the safety of one who comes seeking God. The pilgrimage is described as owed to God by those able to make the journey. Being able is named in the same breath. The closing clause is unexpectedly gentle in its logic. God has no need of anyone.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the section arguing about which sanctuary came first. Classical commentaries place the ayah before the community had access to Mecca, which was still closed to them. So the passage describes a journey its first hearers could not yet make. That timing is part of how the sources read it. The description came well before the opportunity did.

keyTerms.note: A noun of place from the verb to stand. It names the spot where someone stood rather than a monument, so the sign is a location marked by an act rather than by anything built on it.
From the root that gives Arabic its words for faith and for trust. Safety and belief share a root, so entering the house in security and entering it in faith are covered by one word family.
From a root meaning to be rich and to do without. It states that God gains nothing from any of this, which places the whole practice on the side of the one performing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The sanctuary could not be violated, and that was the one reliable truce in Arabia. Men who would kill each other on the open road stood side by side inside its bounds. Traders travelled to its seasons under a safety no tribe would break. Blood feuds paused there. That security was the peninsula's most valuable arrangement. Even those who kept idols inside the house respected it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase used here for the standing place of Abraham occurs twice in the Quran. It appears in this ayah and in an earlier surah. There the instruction is to take it as a place of prayer. Both times it is attached to the same sanctuary. No description of how it looks is given anywhere in the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The closing clause is the striking part. The passage describes a journey people make at real cost. Then it says God has no need of any of it. That takes the exchange out of the picture entirely. Nothing is being supplied to God. So whatever the journey achieves happens inside the one who makes it. The security promised at the house works the same way, received rather than earned.

crossReferences.why: Names the same standing place and instructs that it be taken as a place of prayer.
Describes the call going out, and people arriving from every deep mountain pass.
States the same point generally: you are the needy ones, and God is free of need.

studies.applyIt: Notice the phrase about God having no need of any of it. Whatever you do today that you think of as religious, nothing is being delivered to anyone. It changes the flavour of an act to remember that its whole effect lands on you. Hold one small practice today with that in mind and see what shifts.
studies.explainEasier: Inside the house are clear signs, like the place where Abraham stood. Anyone who enters is safe. People who can make the journey owe this trip to God. God needs nothing from anyone.

studies.title: Why Turn Others Away
studies.meaning: Two questions are put in parallel, each opening with an instruction to speak. The first asks why the signs are refused when God witnesses what is done. The second asks something heavier. Why turn those who have believed away from God's path, seeking to put a bend in it. Early scholars note the shift from a person's own refusal to their effect on others. They also note that both questions close by naming God as watching, not by naming a consequence.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the surah's address to the scriptural communities of the city. Classical commentaries link this section to efforts to unsettle the young community. Old tribal quarrels were reopened. Doubts were raised about the new direction of prayer. Reports of the single events vary. So the sources read the ayat as a pattern of behaviour rather than one episode.

keyTerms.note: The verb for barring someone from a road, used of physical obstruction as well as of dissuading. It names an effect on another person's movement rather than on their opinion.
A noun for a bend or a warp, used of a stick that will not lie straight. Applied to a path it means introducing a deviation, so the road still leads somewhere but no longer where it did.
The plural of one who testifies and one who is present. The word is used of the people addressed and, in the singular, of God two lines earlier, which sets two kinds of witnessing against each other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A road in Arabia could be spoiled without being closed. Moving a cairn, filling a well, or giving a traveller a slightly wrong bearing sent a caravan into country it could not cross. Nobody had to block anything. Deviation was the cheap and deniable form of obstruction, and everyone who travelled knew how small an alteration it took.
studies.didYouKnow: Both ayat close on God's awareness rather than on a threat. They use two different wordings. One says that God witnesses what is done. The other says that God is not unaware of it. The second is a double negative, which Arabic uses to say a thing more strongly than the plain positive would.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates refusing something yourself from stopping someone else reaching it. It treats the second as the graver matter, by giving it the longer question. That implies a duty reaching past your own commitments. It reaches to the effect you have on other people's. Both questions end on being watched rather than on punishment. That leaves the weight where this surah usually places it, in being seen.

crossReferences.why: Names those who disbelieve and turn others from the path of God, joining the two acts.
Describes those who bar others from God's way and seek to make it crooked, in similar words.
Uses the same pair of verbs of those who bar from the path and want a bend in it.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between not doing something yourself and making it harder for somebody else. Think of a person in your life who is trying to get more serious about something good. Notice whether your reaction has made that easier for them, or slightly more awkward. Then adjust one small thing about how you respond next time.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the messenger to put two things to the people of the book. They turn away from God's signs while God watches them do it. They also try to keep other believers off God's road.

studies.title: Who You Listen To
studies.meaning: The address turns, and it is now the believers being spoken to. The warning is not about argument but about going along. If you comply with a party of those given the Book, they will send you back after your belief. Early scholars note the verb, which means returning a thing the way it came. They note the limit to a party rather than a whole community, which this surah keeps throughout. What is described is influence, not force.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. Classical commentaries link this ayah and the ones after it to one incident. Old hostilities between the two main tribes of Medina were deliberately revived. It nearly led to fighting between people who had only recently made peace. The reports agree on the shape of the episode while differing on details. The passage about holding to God's rope, three ayat later, is read as its answer.

keyTerms.note: The verb for willing compliance, from a root meaning to do something readily. It describes going along with someone rather than being persuaded by them, which is why the warning chooses it.
From the root meaning to return a thing to where it came from. It pictures a reversal as a journey retraced rather than as a new position somebody has arrived at.
One of the limiting words this surah uses repeatedly. Its presence keeps the warning attached to particular people acting in a particular way, rather than to a whole community.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The two great tribes of Medina had fought a long and exhausting war before the community formed, ending only a few years earlier. The grievances were fresh, the dead were remembered by name, and men who now prayed together had faced one another in the field. Reviving that memory required no invention at all. It only required someone to raise it at the right moment.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah opens a short passage holding one of the most quoted lines in the surah. That line tells people to hold fast to God's rope together and not to separate. The warning and the remedy stand three ayat apart. Early scholars read them as a single unit answering one incident.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage names going along, not arguing, as the point of danger. A person can hear a case out and stay unmoved. But going along with someone changes what they become. So the choice of whom to follow matters in itself, before any claim is examined. The remedy the surah supplies a few lines later is social rather than intellectual.

crossReferences.why: Gives the answer three ayat later: hold to God's rope together, and do not separate.
Shows people on that day saying they obeyed their chiefs, and were led off the path.
Describes regret over a companion who turned someone away after the reminder had come.

studies.applyIt: Think about whose approval you actually adjust yourself for. Not who you admire, but who you would soften a position in front of. Everyone has someone. Name one, and recall what you last altered because of them. This passage is not asking you to cut anyone off, only to watch the mechanism working.
studies.explainEasier: God speaks to the believers here. If they go along with some of the people who were given the book, those people will pull them back. They would lose the faith they already have.

studies.title: Hold On Until The End
studies.meaning: The passage asks how anyone could reject, when the revelation is being recited among them and the Messenger is present. The question is really a reproach. The answer comes in the same breath, as a remedy. Whoever takes firm hold of God has been guided to a straight path. The next line raises the standard, asking for reverence as it is due. Then it attaches that to the moment of death. So the instruction is about lasting, not about starting.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. The classical sources tie this passage to a specific incident. Someone tried to reopen the old feud between the two main Arab clans of Medina by reciting poetry about a battle they had fought before the migration. The reports describe men reaching for weapons before the quarrel was calmed. These ayat and the ones right after them came down in that setting, which is why they turn at once to unity.

keyTerms.note: The verb for gripping something to save yourself, used of clinging to a rock or a rope. It implies a body in danger rather than a mind in agreement, and it returns two ayat later as a command.

Literally the due of being mindful of Him. The construction sets no measurable limit, and early scholars note that a later ayah, telling believers to be mindful as far as they are able, is read alongside it.

The instruction is not to die but to be in this condition whenever death comes. Arabic can express that with a single participle, which is why the line reads as a command about continuity rather than about dying.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The two clans being addressed had fought a war within living memory. Many men in the mosque had lost fathers or brothers on the other side. Feuds in that culture were kept alive by recitation. A poem naming a killing held an obligation open for generations. One well-chosen verse recited in a marketplace could restart a conflict that had cost hundreds of lives. That is exactly what these ayat interrupted.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for taking firm hold turns up again as a direct command two ayat later. There the community is told to hold to the rope of God together and not to divide. Early scholars read the pair as one movement. The individual grip is described first, then the same grip is made collective, with the incident behind them supplying the reason.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reverence is set at an unlimited standard. It is then tied to endurance rather than intensity. That shifts the whole demand from peaks to continuity. Placing the instruction at the moment of death, which nobody can schedule, means it can only be met by being in that state always. And the remedy offered for wavering is not more effort. It is attachment: holding on to something outside yourself.

crossReferences.why: Turns the individual grip into a collective one and names the feud that these ayat healed.
Instructs mindfulness of God as far as you are able, read alongside the standard set here.
Shows Jacob giving his sons the same charge, not to die except in surrender to God.

studies.applyIt: Ask what you are currently holding on to when things get difficult: a person, a plan, a distraction. Name it honestly, without deciding it is wrong. Then choose one moment in the coming week, when the difficulty arrives, to reach for prayer first instead. The word used here is about grip, and grip is trained by repetition rather than resolved by decision.
studies.explainEasier: God asks how people can turn away when His words are being read to them. Hold on to God and you stay on the right road. Stay that way right up to the end of your life.

studies.title: The Rope And The Pit
studies.meaning: One command with two halves: hold on together, and do not fracture. The word for holding is the same one used for gripping a rock above a drop. Then the reasoning arrives as memory rather than argument. You were enemies, He joined your hearts, and by that favour you became brothers. The final image is a ledge above a fire pit and a hand pulling you back, which makes the previous hostility a survived catastrophe rather than an unfortunate past.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, and this is one of the more securely reported occasions in it. The classical sources describe an attempt to revive the memory of a battle fought between Medina's two main Arab clans before the migration. They describe the anger it raised in men who had been reconciled only a few years earlier. These ayat came down to that gathering. The word for brothers in the ayah described a relationship those men had recently been fighting against.

keyTerms.note: A rope let down to someone below, used in Arabic for a pact of protection between tribes. Early scholars gloss it as the Quran, as the covenant, or as both, and record the range without deciding.
A reflexive form: the splitting is something the group does to itself. Arabic marks that grammatically, so the warning is against self-inflicted fracture rather than against being divided by others.
The verb for making things familiar and joining them into a whole, related to the word for composing a book. It describes intimacy created rather than a truce imposed, which is the ayah's claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina before the migration had been a town at war with itself. The two main Arab clans had fought for years, with the last major battle within living memory of most adults in the mosque. Alliances with the town's other communities had shifted through it. Men praying in the same row had killed each other's relatives. The word brothers in this ayah was not sentimental language; it named a recent and improbable fact.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of a rope reaching down was familiar in a specific legal sense. An agreement of protection extended by a strong tribe to a weaker one was described in exactly that language. Early scholars note that the picture therefore carries an obligation on both sides. The party holding the rope is bound by the pact as well as saved by it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Unity is credited to God, not to human bargaining. That makes division a form of ingratitude as well as a political failure. The passage also recasts a community making peace as a rescue. That raises the stakes a long way. And the rope is single. So the togetherness is not a deal between the parties but a result of what each one is holding.

crossReferences.why: States that no wealth could have joined these hearts, and that God did it.
Names believers as brothers and instructs reconciliation between them as the response.
Gives the individual version of the same grip, in the ayat immediately before this one.

studies.applyIt: Think of one relationship in your community that was repaired and has quietly started fraying again. A family branch, a group of friends, people at your mosque. Do the small, unglamorous thing this week, the message or the visit, before the fraying becomes a position. The ayah treats division as a fire. You have already been pulled back from it once.
studies.explainEasier: Hold on to God together and do not split apart. Remember that you used to be enemies. God brought your hearts together and made you brothers. You were at the edge of a fire and He pulled you back.

studies.title: A Group That Calls To Good
studies.meaning: A group is to exist within the community with three tasks: calling to what is good, urging what is recognised as right, and holding people back from what is wrong. The order matters, since the invitation comes before either instruction. Those who do this are named as the ones who succeed. The second line gives the warning by contrast. It points to communities that split and argued after clear evidence had reached them. So the danger is put in division, not in ignorance.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. These lines come straight after the ayat that healed a near-fatal quarrel between Medina's two main Arab clans. Early scholars read the placement as the constructive half of that episode. Having stopped the community from breaking apart, the passage gives it a task. The reference to those who divided after clear proofs reached them is generally read as pointing to earlier communities, not to any group in the town.

keyTerms.note: A group with a shared purpose rather than a shared ancestry. The Quran uses it of nations, of religious communities, and once of a single man, so its size is set by its function.
From the root for knowing. It names good that a society already acknowledges, which grounds the work in shared understanding rather than in a standard the audience has never heard.
The exact opposite construction, from the root for denying or failing to recognise. The pair frames moral work as reminding people of what they know rather than as introducing something foreign.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina had no police force and no standing court. Order was kept by clan elders and by public reputation. It was also kept by ordinary men willing to speak up in a market or a courtyard when something was wrong. A community that would not correct itself had nothing else to fall back on. Giving this work to a group within the town described something the audience already knew. It was the difference between a working settlement and a lawless one.
studies.didYouKnow: The paired terms for recognised good and rejected wrong occur together in nine ayat of the Quran. The pairing became the standard name for a whole field of Islamic writing on right conduct. Early scholars debated the grammar of this ayah. Some read the group described as a special part of the community. Others read it as the community as a whole. Both readings survive.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Moral duty is shown as shared and organised, not left to each person's conscience. That makes the health of a community a religious matter. Putting the invitation first sets the tone. The work begins by calling people toward something. It does not begin by stopping them. And the failure named is division after clear evidence. So unity is treated as a condition for the work, not a reward for it.

crossReferences.why: Attributes the same three tasks to the community as a whole and calls it brought forth for humanity.
Sets out how the calling is to be done: with wisdom, good instruction, and the better argument.
Names urging one another to truth and to patience as what saves people from loss.

studies.applyIt: The next time you see something wrong in a group you belong to, start with the first of the three tasks rather than the third. Say what the better thing would look like before you say what is wrong with the current one. It is slower and it works more often. This ayah puts the invitation first for a reason.
studies.explainEasier: Some people in every community should call others to do good. They should speak up against wrong. Do not be like the groups who broke apart and argued after the truth was made clear to them.

studies.title: Faces On That Day
studies.meaning: A day is described entirely through faces. Some are made bright and some are darkened. Nothing is said about what produced either. Then the second group is addressed with a question that is really a reminder: did you refuse after your belief. Early scholars note that the imagery comes from ordinary Arabic usage. A bright face means relief and being proved right. A darkened one means grief and disgrace. So what is described is a condition becoming visible.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the instruction to hold together and the warning about division. Classical commentaries read the imagery as the outcome of the argument before it. The question put to the darkened faces repeats wording used earlier in the surah. That earlier wording was about refusal after belief. No occasion is reported. The passage works as the close of a longer run.

keyTerms.note: A verb of colour change used in Arabic idiom for a face lit by relief or joy. It describes brightness rather than pigment, and the same root is used elsewhere of eyes dimmed by weeping.
The counterpart verb. In Arabic usage a face darkening names grief, shame or dread, and the Quran uses the same idiom elsewhere of a man receiving news he does not want.
The verb for tasting, used of experiencing something directly and personally. It makes the consequence something known from the inside rather than observed, which is why the Quran uses it here.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Faces did the work of documents in Arabia. Judgements were given in gatherings. A man's outcome was read off him as he walked back to his people, before he had said anything. Everyone present knew what a returning face meant. In a society with no written verdicts, the face was where a decision became public. That is why the image needed no explaining.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran uses this same pair of colour verbs for faces in a later surah. There they describe those who lied about God. It uses the darkening idiom elsewhere, of a man told he has a daughter. The imagery belongs to ordinary Arabic speech before it belongs to any scene of judgement.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage describes an outcome without describing a verdict. What appears on that day is a condition becoming visible, not a sentence being read out. That suggests the state already exists and is only uncovered. It is a different picture from a trial whose result is in doubt. The question put to the darkened faces backs that up. They are asked to recognise something, not told it.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other half immediately: those with bright faces are inside God's mercy, remaining.
Describes faces on that day radiant and looking, and others drawn and expecting disaster.
Pairs bright laughing faces with faces covered over by dust and darkness.

studies.applyIt: Faces give people away long before words do. Spend a day noticing your own. Look in a mirror after a hard conversation, or in a dark screen. Not to judge it, only to see what it already tells anyone who looks. This passage assumes a life becomes visible in the end. Some of that showing begins early.
studies.explainEasier: On that day some faces will be bright and some will be dark. The dark ones will be asked if they gave up their faith after they had it. Then they will taste what follows.

studies.title: God Desires No Injustice
studies.meaning: The other half of the scene arrives in a single clause. The phrasing is spatial. Those with bright faces are inside God's mercy, and they remain there. Mercy is described as a place rather than a feeling. The passage then steps back twice. It says these are God's signs, recited in truth, and that God wants no injustice for anyone. Then it says everything in the heavens and the earth belongs to Him, and all matters return to Him.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the long section that ran from the warning about division to the imagery of faces. Classical commentaries treat these three ayat as a summary. They cover everything argued since the surah's discussion with the scriptural communities began. The ayat state the principle under all of it. Then they place the whole matter in God's hands.

keyTerms.note: A preposition of containment. Mercy is described as something entered and remained within, which turns an attribute into a location, and the Quran uses the same construction of gardens.
The phrase covers truth, reality and due right together. Reciting with it means both that the content is accurate and that the reciting is properly done, and the commentators keep both senses.
A passive verb with a plural noun covering affairs, commands and situations. Nothing is said about who does the returning, which leaves the process impersonal and only the destination named.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everything in Arabian life went somewhere in the end to be settled. Disputes went to a judge. Debts went to a reckoning. A caravan went to its destination. Nothing was simply left open, because an unsettled matter meant danger that carried on. So the idea that all affairs go somewhere to be decided was not abstract. It described how their world already ran.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that all matters return to God appears several times in the Quran. It always comes at the end of a passage, never at its opening. Early scholars note that placement. The formula works as a closing rather than a starting point. It marks where an argument has finished.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The middle ayah carries the weight of the three. After a scene of judgement, the passage says God wants no injustice for anyone at all. That frames everything just described as the outcome of what people did. It is not the outcome of what was wished on them. Placing that line between the scene and the claim of ownership matters. It keeps the ownership from being read as power used at whim.

crossReferences.why: Gives the other half of this scene, the darkened faces and the question put to them.
Says God does not wrong by the weight of an atom, and multiplies whatever is good.
Repeats the same principle in different words: God wills no injustice for the servants.

studies.applyIt: Read the middle sentence on its own: God desires no injustice for anyone. If you carry a suspicion that things are stacked against you, sit with that line for a minute rather than arguing with it. You do not have to resolve anything today. Notice only whether you actually believe it, and answer honestly.
studies.explainEasier: The people with bright faces are inside God's mercy, and they stay there. These are God's signs, read out truly. God wants nothing unfair for anyone. Everything belongs to Him, and everything goes back to Him.

studies.title: The Best Community And Its Conditions
studies.meaning: The superlative arrives with conditions attached. Three clauses follow it: urging good, forbidding wrong, and believing in God. Early scholars read them as the grounds of the ranking, not decoration on it. The opening verb is in the past tense. Scholars differ over whether that means the community was so in God's knowledge from the beginning, or is being reminded what it was brought out to do. The final line then refuses a blanket verdict on others.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina. Much of it deals with the community's relations with the People of the Scripture there. It also deals with its recovery after the defeat at Uhud. The ayah sits in a run of passages contrasting a community held together by a shared job with one broken by rivalry. Early scholars report no single agreed occasion for it, and read it in the flow of that argument.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a mother or a source. It names a body of people bound by something they share, a direction, a calling, a moment in time, rather than by descent.
A passive verb of being drawn out or made to emerge, used elsewhere of crops pushed up from the soil. The community is not self-made; it is described as something raised for a purpose.
Literally the known, the familiar. It covers what sound human sense already recognises as decent, so the good being urged is not exotic; it is what people already acknowledge when they are honest.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In Medina a person's standing came from family line. Which clan, which alliance, how many fighting men could be called to a quarrel. Rank was something you inherited and defended with poetry and raids. Meccan emigrants, Medinan hosts and clans lately at war with each other were now told their rank lay in what they did, not in who they came from. That was a genuinely strange arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The ayah is bracketed by qualifications on both sides. Its own last clause says that some of the People of the Scripture believe, and three ayat later the surah states outright that they are not all alike, describing a group among them who recite through the night and prostrate. The generalisation is never left standing on its own.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Excellence here is about function, not essence. A community is ranked by an activity it can stop doing. So the description can be lost as well as held. The order matters too. Two duties towards other people come before the mention of belief. So faith is shown leading to public duty rather than sitting apart from it. And the qualification about others keeps the claim from hardening into contempt.

crossReferences.why: States the same commission as a duty for a group within the community, a few ayat earlier.
Calls the community a middle nation set as witnesses over people, the same commissioning language.
Immediately corrects any blanket reading by naming an upright group among the People of the Scripture.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing this week that you would normally let pass: a rumour repeated in a group chat, a colleague spoken about unfairly. Say something, briefly and without heat, and then let it go. The ayah ties the community's worth to small interventions like that one, made by people who would rather have stayed quiet.
studies.explainEasier: God tells this community they are the best one raised up for people. But that comes with a job. They tell people to do good, warn them away from wrong, and believe in God.

studies.title: No Harm Beyond Insult
studies.meaning: A limit is placed on what opposition can achieve. The harm is said to reach no further than words that wound. If it comes to fighting, the outcome is named in advance. Early scholars read the passage as reassurance given at a particular moment. They do not read it as a general rule about every future encounter. They also note the word chosen for the harm. It covers annoyance and injury of a kind that does not reach the vital parts.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, following the passage describing the community as raised up for the good of people. Classical commentaries place these ayat in a time of pressure from groups in and around the city. They read them as addressed to a community with real reason to feel outnumbered. The reassurance is specific to that setting. The surah shortly afterwards turns to a battle that went badly.

keyTerms.note: A word for harm that irritates and wounds without destroying. The Quran uses it of insult, of discomfort and of minor injury, so it names a category of damage rather than a degree of it.
An idiom for fleeing, built from the word for a back. Arabic describes a retreat by what the pursuer sees, which is more vivid than the abstract word for flight would be.
The passive of the verb for coming to someone's aid, from the same root used earlier in this surah of the disciples. The passive form leaves the absent helper entirely unnamed.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Insult was a weapon in Arabia, and a serious one. Satirical poetry could damage a tribe's standing for a generation, and poets were employed for exactly that purpose. Being told that opposition would go no further than words was no small reassurance to that audience. Words were the instrument they most feared after the sword, and sometimes before it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for harm appears more than twenty times in the Quran. It covers things as different as verbal abuse, physical discomfort, and the injury done by a boastful gift. Its range is wide enough that the early Arabic dictionary writers define it partly by what it leaves out. It is damage that does not destroy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage sets a boundary around what opposition can do. That is different from promising that none will come. Insult and irritation are granted outright. The claim is about where the damage stops. That is a particular kind of comfort. It neither denies the difficulty nor treats it as decisive. It leaves a person free to feel the sting without drawing a conclusion from it.

crossReferences.why: Says plainly that you will hear much hurt, and joins it to patience and mindfulness.
Tells the Prophet to disregard the hurt they cause, and to rely on God instead.
Names giving followed by no reminder and no hurt as the giving that keeps its reward.

studies.applyIt: Someone will say something to you this week that stings and changes nothing. Notice the gap between how much it hurts and how much it actually does. Those two quantities are almost never the same, and this ayah's whole comfort lies in keeping them apart. Name the second one out loud; it usually turns out to be small.
studies.explainEasier: These people cannot really hurt you. They can only say things that sting. If they fight you, they will turn and run away. And no one will come to help them.

studies.title: Except By Two Ropes
studies.meaning: A state of humiliation and hardship is described as having settled over a community in the past. The causes are named inside the ayah itself. Refusing God's signs. Killing prophets. Disobedience and going too far. Two exceptions are stated in the middle of it, both called ropes. One comes from God and one from people. Early scholars read them as a covenant with God and a bond of protection or treaty with other human beings. So the way out is named alongside the condition.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in a section that moves between description and qualification. Classical commentaries read the passage as an account of a past condition attached to named conduct. They do not read it as a permanent verdict on any people. The very next ayah says plainly that they are not all alike. It describes an upright community among them. The sources treat that as part of how this ayah is read.

keyTerms.note: A passive verb used of pitching a tent over a place. The image is of something set up above and around people, so the condition is described as a covering rather than as a quality they possess.
The word for a rope, used in Arabic for a covenant or a protection agreement. The same image appears a few ayat earlier in this surah, where believers are told to hold to God's rope together.
From the root that gives Arabic its word for the poor and for stillness. It names an inability to move or improve one's position rather than poverty measured as a bare quantity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection deals were the fabric of Arabian security. A group without a treaty was exposed everywhere it went. A group with a bond could travel and trade in safety. Such deals were spoken of as ropes and as ties. Everyone knew that the gap between a safe life and an exposed one was often one arrangement with a stronger party.
studies.didYouKnow: The image of a rope appears twice within ten ayat of this surah. Once it is the rope of God that believers are told to hold to together. Once it is here, as the exception to a described condition. The same everyday word carries a promise in one place and a way out in the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah states causes rather than declaring a nature. That is what lets the next ayah say plainly that they are not all alike. Read together, the two make a claim about how consequences work. Conduct is named. Its effects are described. The description is at once stopped from hardening into a label. The exception clauses do the same work from inside the ayah.

crossReferences.why: Follows immediately and says they are not alike, describing an upright community among them.
Uses the same image of a rope from God, as what believers are to hold to together.
Describes the same condition and names the same causes, in an earlier surah's account.

studies.applyIt: Notice that the ayah names causes and then, one line later, refuses to let the description become a label. That is a discipline worth borrowing. When you find yourself explaining a whole group by a pattern, say the next sentence too: they are not all alike. Say it out loud, and mean it about a specific person you know.
studies.explainEasier: This community was covered with shame and hard times. The ayah says why: they refused God's signs and killed prophets. But two things could protect them. A bond with God, and a bond with people.

studies.title: They Are Not All Alike
studies.meaning: A short clause opens the ayah and revises everything before it: they are not alike. What follows is entirely positive. It describes an upright community among the People of the Book. They recite God's verses through the hours of the night, and they prostrate. Early scholars note the word for upright, which describes something standing firm. They note the choice of the night hours, which puts the practice where nobody is watching. Nothing in the description is hedged.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, right after a passage describing a condition and its causes. Classical commentaries treat the placement as the point of the ayah. It stops the description before it from being made general. Some sources connect it to members of the scriptural communities of Medina who had joined the young community. Others read it more broadly. The praise itself is not disputed.

keyTerms.note: A word for evenness, used of a level surface and of two things of the same measure. Denying it says the members of a group are not interchangeable, which is a claim about internal variety.
A noun for a body of people joined to a participle meaning standing. The image is of standing firm and standing in prayer at the same time, and the commentators keep both senses in view.
A plural noun for the successive portions of the night. Naming them in the plural suggests recitation spread across the night rather than confined to one vigil at a fixed hour.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The night belonged to whoever chose it. Lamps were expensive, oil was rationed, and most households went dark shortly after the evening meal. Anyone reciting through the hours of darkness was spending a resource and losing sleep before a working day. It was the least visible and most costly kind of devotion, and nobody would know unless a neighbour happened to hear.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah begins one of the Quran's most direct refusals to generalise. The passage it opens runs for three ayat of praise with no conditions. The word for community used here is the same one the surah applies a few ayat earlier to the believers themselves. That places both groups under one term.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The refusal to make it general is a matter of accuracy, not of manners. A group's conduct is described. At once the text says the group is not all one thing. That treats even a fair criticism as incomplete without it. The praise that follows matters too. It is given for acts anyone would call devotion. No condition of membership is attached.

crossReferences.why: Describes the condition this ayah immediately qualifies, one line earlier in the surah.
Closes the surah by describing those among the People of the Book who believe with humility.
Describes those nearest in affection to the believers, and their tears on hearing revelation.

studies.applyIt: Find one group you hold a settled opinion about, and think of a specific person inside it who does not fit. Not as a rhetorical exercise: an actual person with a name. Hold both facts at once, the pattern you noticed and the individual who contradicts it. This ayah's whole method is insisting both stay in the sentence.
studies.explainEasier: Not everyone is the same. Among the people of the book there is a group that stands firm. They read God's words during the night hours. And they bow down low in prayer.

studies.title: Quick To The Good
studies.meaning: The praise continues and becomes a list. Belief in God and the Last Day. Urging what is recognised as right. Holding back what is wrong. Hurrying toward good deeds. The verb for hurrying is the striking one, since it describes competing rather than merely doing. A guarantee follows: whatever good they do will not be denied them. Early scholars note that these are exactly the qualities the surah gives the believing community a few ayat earlier.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. It sits in the passage that refuses to lump the People of the Book together. These two ayat finish a picture. The picture began with an upright group reciting through the night. The qualities named are the same ones the surah already gives the believers. Classical commentaries read the repeat as meant, not chance.

keyTerms.note: A passive participle from the verb to know. It names what a sound conscience already recognises, so the good being urged is described as familiar rather than newly imposed from outside.
The counterpart term, from a root meaning to find something strange or to deny it. Wrong is named as what the same conscience refuses, which pairs the two words as recognition and its opposite.
A form of the verb to hurry that carries competition. It describes not merely speed but eagerness measured against others, so the good is pursued rather than simply performed.
From the root meaning to cover over, used elsewhere in this surah of refusing signs. Applied to a reward it means having a deed covered up and left unacknowledged by anyone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Recognition was the currency of a small society. A man who acted well in a public matter expected it to be remembered. A slight stayed unforgotten for a generation. Being denied credit for something you did was among the deepest injuries in that world. In some ways it was worse than losing property. A name could not be rebuilt by working harder.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs for urging the good and holding back the wrong appear together as a fixed pair throughout the Quran. This surah gives them to the believing community a few ayat earlier. The same formula is used here of a group among the People of the Book. That is one of the passage's most deliberate features.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The guarantee is attached to actions rather than to belonging. Good done will not go unacknowledged, and the doer's community is never mentioned. Read alongside the same description of the believers a few lines earlier, the effect is clear. The qualities themselves are what count. The closing clause says God knows the mindful. That puts the accounting beyond human sorting.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same three qualities of the believing community, a few ayat earlier in this surah.
Describes prophets racing toward good deeds and calling on God in hope and in awe.
Instructs everyone to compete in good works, wherever it is that they turn.

studies.applyIt: Pick the good thing you have been meaning to do and keep rescheduling. The verb here is about racing. The enemy of racing is putting off, not laziness. Do the smaller version today rather than the better version next month. Notice how much of the delay was about wanting it to look impressive.
studies.explainEasier: They believe in God and the last day. They tell people to do good and to stay away from wrong. They rush to do good things. Whatever good they do will be counted.

studies.title: Said Again, Ending Elsewhere
studies.meaning: The sentence is almost the one this surah used a hundred ayat earlier. The difference lies at the end. There the closing image was fuel. Here it is company, describing those addressed as the people of the Fire who remain in it. Early scholars note that the surah repeats wordings at intervals with changed endings. They read the change as marking how far the argument has travelled between the two. It is not variation without purpose.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, right after the passage praising an upright group among the People of the Book. The placement is deliberate. A warm description is followed at once by a warning. The warning is addressed to a group defined by refusal, not to any community. Classical commentaries treat the pairing as this surah's way of stopping either statement from being read on its own.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a close associate or a travelling companion. Arabic uses it for those permanently attached to a place or a condition, so the phrase describes belonging rather than location.
From a root meaning to persist and to endure without change. It describes duration without alteration, which is why the same word is used of both the garden and the fire in this surah.
Named with the definite article, as a known thing rather than as a description. The Quran generally uses it this way, assuming that the referent is understood rather than introducing it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Belonging in Arabia was expressed in exactly this form. A man was named as one of the people of a valley, a well or a tribe. That phrase told you where he could travel safely and who would answer for him. Being called the companions of something stated who you were, not where you were. The audience heard it in that register.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah repeats an earlier one in the same surah almost word for word. Only its closing image changes. Surah 3 does this several times, restating a wording after a long stretch of other material. The repeats are one of the ways the chapter holds a long and varied argument together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Placing this right after praise of people outside the community does something specific. Neither the praise nor the warning is handed out by group. The ayat before praised without any conditions. This one warns without naming anyone. What decides the outcome in both cases is described entirely in terms of conduct and refusal. That is the surah's steady position.

crossReferences.why: States the same claim almost word for word earlier in this surah, closing on a different image.
Supplies the commendation of an upright group that this warning immediately follows.
Repeats the same formula about wealth and children availing nothing against God.

studies.applyIt: Notice how the surah alternates: praise, then warning, then praise again, never letting either settle into a verdict about a group. If you tend to read scripture looking for confirmation about who is in and who is out, this stretch is built to make that difficult. Read the four ayat around this one in order.
studies.explainEasier: Some people turn away from God. Their money will not help them when they stand before Him. Their children will not help them either. They belong to the Fire, and they will stay there.

studies.title: A Wind With Frost In It
studies.meaning: A comparison is drawn for what is spent without anything behind it. It is like a wind carrying bitter cold that reaches a standing crop and destroys it. The detail that matters is what was lost: not seed, but a harvest, something already grown and nearly ready to cut. Classical commentators note the closing clause, which turns the loss inward. God did not wrong them; the wrong was already in the field, since the owners are described as having wronged themselves before the wind arrived.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, in the section describing those who oppose the community. Classical commentaries link the parable to spending done for reputation or for advantage. That includes money spent on campaigns against the young community. The Quran names no occasion. The sources treat the comparison as general, since its point is about the link between an act and what stands behind it.

keyTerms.note: A word for intense cold, from a root also connected with a persistent sound and with tying something tightly. It names cold as something that grips rather than merely as a lowered temperature.
The word for cultivated ground and what grows on it, used earlier in this surah among the things people love. It covers the labour that went in as well as the crop that came up.
The object is placed before the verb, a construction Arabic uses for emphasis. The word order insists that the wronged party and the one doing the wrong are the same people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A crop lost late was the worst kind of loss. Seed that failed cost a season's seed; a standing harvest destroyed days before cutting cost the seed, the water, the labour and the whole year's food. Frost was the specific fear on higher ground, arriving in one night without warning. Everyone farming knew families ruined in exactly that way.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used for the tilled field in this parable appears earlier in this same surah. There it sits in the list of things made attractive to people. The Quran often reuses a term across a chapter in different roles. Here one word names both something loved and something destroyed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The parable places the failure before the disaster. A wind destroys the crop, but the ayah says the wrong was already done. It was done by the owners to themselves. That makes the loss a disclosure rather than a punishment. What happens reveals what the spending actually was. An act done for the wrong reason was never carrying what its owner believed it carried.

crossReferences.why: Compares a gift given for show to soil on a rock washed bare by heavy rain.
Compares the deeds of those who refused to ashes blown apart by wind on a stormy day.
Describes deeds turned into scattered dust once they are finally brought forward.

studies.applyIt: Think of something good you did recently and ask, honestly, what you were hoping would follow from it. Not to spoil it, and not to conclude that you should stop. Just notice the answer. This parable is about what stands behind an act, and that is usually easier to see in a small case than a large one.
studies.explainEasier: What these people spend is like a freezing wind. The wind hits a field of grain that is ready and kills it. God did not treat them unfairly. They did the harm to themselves.

studies.title: Confidants From Outside
studies.meaning: The word translated here as friends means the lining of a garment. It names an inner circle, the people close enough to know what is not said in public. The warning is about letting into that circle people who wish you harm. The description is precise. They will not stop short of ruining you. They would like to see you strained. Hostility has already surfaced in their speech, and what is hidden is greater. The passage closes by saying the signs have been made plain, if you use reason.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at a time when the community's plans and inner affairs were of real interest to groups opposed to it. Classical commentaries read the ayah as being about private counsel, not about ordinary dealings. They note that the Quran elsewhere calls for kindness and fairness toward those who have not fought the community. The wording itself draws that line.

keyTerms.note: The word for the inner lining of a garment, the layer that sits against the skin. Used of people it names close confidants, so the warning concerns access rather than acquaintance.
A noun covering corruption, confusion and loss of one's senses. It names damage that spoils the working of a thing rather than destroying the thing outright.
From a root meaning to be strained or brought into difficulty, used of a bone breaking after it had begun to set. It names distress arising from pressure rather than from a single blow.
An intensive form from the root for hatred. Its appearance is described as having already surfaced in speech, which is what makes the concealed portion something a listener can infer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city the size of Medina, a household's private business travelled at the speed of one conversation. Plans for a journey. A marriage being arranged. A debt coming due. The movements of a caravan. All of it had value to somebody. There were no locked archives. Who you spoke freely in front of was the whole information policy open to a family or a community.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for an inner circle comes from the language of clothing. It names the lining that sits against the body. Arabic uses its counterpart for the outer face of a garment. The pair gives the language a way of separating what is close and hidden from what is put on show.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates the people you deal with from the people you confide in. The warning falls only on the second. That leaves ordinary relations untouched. It treats access to a community's private counsel as a matter of judgement rather than of goodwill. Ending on reason rather than on obedience matters too. It frames the instruction as something to be understood, not simply followed.

crossReferences.why: Instructs kindness and fairness toward those who did not fight you over religion.
Continues immediately, describing an affection that runs in only one direction.
Uses the same word for an inner circle, in a passage about who is taken into confidence.

studies.applyIt: There is a difference between who you are kind to and who you tell things to. Most people manage the first carefully and the second by accident. Think about the last thing you were genuinely worried about and who ended up hearing it. Ask whether that list was chosen, or simply whoever happened to be nearby.
studies.explainEasier: God tells the believers not to let people who wish them harm into their closest circle. Those people want to see them in trouble. Their dislike already shows in what they say. What they hide is worse.

studies.title: You Love Them, They Do Not
studies.meaning: An imbalance is described, and the believers are not blamed for it. They love people who do not love them back. They accept the whole of scripture, while others do not accept in the same way. Then comes a scene in two settings. Warmth when they meet. Fingers bitten in rage when they are alone. The instruction that follows is brief and uncomfortable. Early scholars read the phrase about dying in one's rage as a statement about how useless that anger is. They do not read it as a curse.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the previous ayah's discussion of who is let into a community's confidence. Classical commentaries place these ayat among groups in Medina whose public conduct differed from their private view. Reports of named people vary. So the surah keeps to the general description, as it does throughout this section. The weight falls on the gap between the two settings.

keyTerms.gloss: they bit their fingertips at you
keyTerms.note: A physical idiom for rage that has found no outlet. Arabic uses it of frustration turned on the self, and the specific noun names the tips of the fingers rather than the hand.
Distinguished by the lexicographers from ordinary anger as the inward heat that has not yet been discharged. It names the feeling itself rather than any act arising out of it.
Literally the owner or substance of the chests. The construction names not merely the contents but the settled disposition beneath them, which is why translators reach for the heart.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Public courtesy was required in Arabian society, and it told you very little. Hospitality was extended to people you meant to fight. Greeting a man warmly in the market said nothing about what you said of him at home. Everyone understood that the two levels ran side by side. What was rare was any way of knowing which one you were in.
studies.didYouKnow: The gesture of biting the fingers in rage appears in the Quran in one other place. There a wrongdoer bites his hands in regret on the Day of Judgement. Both uses describe a body turning frustration on itself. The moment is one when nothing at all can be done about the cause.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage admits an affection that is not returned, and never tells anyone to withdraw it. What is corrected is not the love but the misreading of the situation. The believers are given accurate information rather than a change of heart. The final clause moves the whole matter into God's knowledge. That is this surah's usual way of closing a description of what people conceal.

crossReferences.why: Introduces the same group one ayah earlier, warning against admitting them to confidence.
Uses the same gesture of biting the hands, in regret rather than in rage.
States earlier in this surah that God knows what the chests hold, concealed or disclosed.

studies.applyIt: There is probably someone you like more than they like you. That is ordinary and not a failure on either side. This ayah does not tell the believers to stop caring; it tells them to see the situation accurately. Try holding both facts about one relationship this week, without adjusting the warmth and without pretending.
studies.explainEasier: You care about these people, but they do not care about you. When they meet you they say they believe. When they are alone they bite their fingers in anger. God knows what is in every heart.

studies.title: Their Scheming Will Not Reach You
studies.meaning: A pattern is described first. Your good fortune upsets them, and your misfortune pleases them. Then a condition follows, and it is not a strategy. If you endure and stay mindful, their scheming will not harm you at all. Early scholars note that nothing is said about countering the plan. The protection offered is attached entirely to the conduct of the person threatened. The closing description says God encompasses what they do. That is a claim about scope rather than about response.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the short passage about confidants and hidden hostility. Classical commentaries connect it to the period around the hard day at Uhud. The community's setbacks were watched closely by those hoping for them. The surah turns to that battle in the very next ayah. So this instruction sits right before an account of a real reverse.

keyTerms.note: A verb of light contact, used of one thing brushing against another. It is used here of good fortune while a stronger verb is used of misfortune, a difference the commentators notice.
A verb of hitting a target, stronger than the one used of good fortune in the same sentence. The pairing suggests that difficulty arrives with more force than ease ever does.
A noun for a plan laid quietly, from a root also used of straining and of a trick. It names the arrangement itself rather than any act eventually carried out through it.
An active participle from the verb to surround, used of a wall enclosing a place. It describes knowledge as containment, so nothing done is outside the perimeter of it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a city where everyone's fortunes were public, pleasure at a rival's setback was a known social fact. A failed harvest, a lost caravan or a marriage broken off was discussed everywhere within days. There was no privacy in which to fail. Living well under that kind of watching was a practical problem. People faced it constantly.
studies.didYouKnow: The two verbs used in this ayah for good and bad fortune are deliberately unequal in force. One means to touch lightly. The other means to strike a target. The Quran uses this imbalance in several places. Early scholars read it as reflecting how differently the two are actually felt.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The protection offered depends on the conduct of the one threatened. It does not depend on any action taken against the threat. That moves security out of the outcome of a contest. It puts it into the state of the person exposed. That is a substantial claim. What makes a scheme harmless happens in the target, not in the plan. The closing name keeps the scheme visible without letting it decide anything.

crossReferences.why: Joins the same two qualities, patience and mindfulness, to hearing much hurt from others.
Says God does not guide the scheming of the treacherous through to its intended end.
States that an evil scheme encircles only the people who devise it.

studies.applyIt: Someone is probably pleased about a setback of yours right now. You cannot do anything about that, and trying to is precisely what this ayah declines to recommend. Instead, name the two things it does ask for, endurance and mindfulness, and pick the smaller of the two to work on today.
studies.explainEasier: When something good happens to you, it upsets them. When something bad happens, they are glad. But if you hold on and stay careful, their plans cannot hurt you at all.

studies.title: The Morning You Went Out
studies.meaning: The account of the hard day begins not with the fighting but with a morning. Leaving home, and assigning positions. Then two admissions in quick succession. Two groups among the believers almost lost heart, and the ayah says God was their protector in that very moment. Then a reminder of the earlier victory, won when the community was weak. Then an instruction that closes on thankfulness. Early scholars note that the passage opens its account of a defeat by recalling a victory.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening the surah's long treatment of the battle at Uhud in the third year after the migration. A force from Mecca came to avenge its losses at Badr. The Muslim force met it outside the city. Classical sources agree on the broad course of the day. That includes the near-withdrawal of two groups before the fighting, which the Quran records here without softening it.

keyTerms.gloss: you set out in the morning
keyTerms.note: A verb specific to the early part of the day, from the root that gives Arabic its word for tomorrow. The time of day is built into the verb rather than added on beside it.
From a root meaning to settle someone in a place, used of finding lodging for a traveller. Applied to a battle line it means putting each group where it is meant to stay.
A dual verb from a root covering weakness of resolve and failure of nerve. The dual form is exact, naming two groups and no more, which is why the report cannot be generalised.
The plural of a word for one who is lowly or without power. Used of the earlier battle it concedes the community's own weakness rather than describing anything about its opponents.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A battle in that world was often decided before contact rather than during it. Position, high ground and the discipline of holding a line mattered more than numbers. A force that broke formation was usually finished. Men fought beside relatives, so a single group withdrawing exposed families as well as flanks. Assigning positions in the morning was the most important work of the day.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran names the earlier battle of Badr directly in this passage. It is one of very few places where it names a battlefield at all. Most of its references to specific events describe them without naming them. That makes the naming here unusually direct, inside an account of a later and harder day.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The most striking clause is the one about the two groups who nearly faltered. It says God was their protector in the same breath. Failure of nerve is recorded and not disowned. The relationship is not described as suspended by it. That sets up something the rest of the Uhud section develops. The account can be honest about weakness because the argument does not depend on denying it.

crossReferences.why: Recalls Badr earlier in this surah, describing the two parties and the sign in them.
Describes the appeal for help at Badr and the reinforcement sent as reassurance.
Continues this account, describing the moment the line broke and giving the reason.

studies.applyIt: Notice the shape of this opening: before describing a bad day it recalls a good one, and the weakness that preceded that. When something goes wrong this week, try beginning your account of it in the same place, with what went right before and how thin the margin actually was. It changes what the difficult part means.
studies.explainEasier: Remember the morning you left home to place the believers for battle. Two groups nearly gave up, but God kept them safe. God had already helped you win at Badr when you were weak.

studies.title: Three Thousand Sent Down
studies.meaning: A question is quoted rather than a statement made. Is it not enough for you that your Lord reinforces you with three thousand angels sent down. Early scholars differ over which battle the number belongs to. Some read it of the earlier day at Badr and others of the encounter this passage describes. The sources record the disagreement without settling it. What is not in dispute is the form. Reassurance is offered as a question, which leaves the hearer to answer.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, inside the account of the battle at Uhud. Classical commentaries differ over whether the promise reported here belongs to that day or to the earlier victory at Badr. Both readings are preserved in the major commentaries, along with their evidence. The Quran does not resolve it. The surah moves straight on to a conditional promise of further reinforcement.

keyTerms.note: From the root for sufficiency, the same one behind the phrase God is enough for us that appears later in this surah. It asks about adequacy rather than about what anyone wants.
From a root meaning to stretch or extend, used of a supply line and of ink drawn from a well. Help is pictured as something extended outward rather than simply dropped in.
A passive participle stressing that the reinforcement descends rather than merely arrives. The commentators note that the same root runs through this surah's vocabulary for revelation itself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Numbers in Arabian warfare were known and counted. Before a fight, scouts reported the opposing force. Men then made their own calculations about whether to stand. Three thousand was larger than most armies the peninsula had ever gathered. Naming it named a quantity outside ordinary experience, while still using the terms a fighter would think in.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran gives specific numbers of angels in only a small number of places. Two of them concern battles fought by this community. Elsewhere angelic presence is described with no figure at all. That makes the counted reinforcements in this surah and in Surah 8 unusual within the text.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Offering reassurance as a question puts the work of belief on the hearer. It does not deliver a guarantee. It also frames unseen help as already given rather than promised, since the verb describes reinforcement already under way. So the passage meets fear by supplying information about the present. It does not supply information about the outcome. That is a different kind of comfort from a prediction.

crossReferences.why: Describes the appeal at Badr and a thousand angels sent in succession as the answer.
Raises the number conditionally in the very next ayah, on two stated conditions.
Speaks of forces nobody could see, sent down at a moment when numbers had failed.

studies.applyIt: Notice that this is a question. When you are afraid you probably ask for reassurance. You rarely stop to answer whether what you already have would be enough. Try that today with one specific worry. List what you actually have in hand. Then answer the question honestly instead of moving straight on to asking for more.
studies.explainEasier: The believers were told that their Lord was backing them up. He sent down three thousand angels to help. They were asked whether that was not enough for them.

studies.title: If You Hold And Guard
studies.meaning: The answer to the previous question arrives in one word meaning on the contrary. The promise is then extended with conditions attached. If you hold fast, if you stay mindful, and if they come upon you suddenly, the reinforcement rises to five thousand marked angels. Early scholars discuss the word describing them, which suggests distinguishing marks, and keep more than one explanation. The conditions are the notable part. Unseen help is described as tied to what the people receiving it do.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the account of the battle at Uhud and its promise of help. Classical commentaries differ over whether the promised five thousand were sent. Many read the attached conditions as unmet on that day. The sources keep the discussion carefully. The surah's later account of the battle describes the very failure of nerve those conditions name.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to boil over, used of water and of a sudden surge. It describes an attack arriving at once and without pause, which is why translators reach for the word suddenly.
An active participle from the root for marking, the same one used earlier in this surah of branded horses. Commentators explain it variously as marked in appearance or as marking their targets.
From the root covering binding and restraint. In a battle setting it names holding a position under pressure, which is exactly what the surah's later account says was not done.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Discipline decided engagements in that world. A line that held under archery could win against greater numbers. A line that moved to collect plunder lost the field. Commanders repeated their position orders, because everyone knew how quickly a formation dissolved once men began thinking on their own. The conditions in this ayah are stated in the words of exactly that problem.
studies.didYouKnow: The number in this ayah rises from the one before it, three thousand to five thousand. The increase arrives with conditions the earlier figure did not carry. Early scholars treat the conditional structure as significant. Much of their discussion concerns whether the larger reinforcement was ever sent.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage attaches unseen help to human conduct without making it a payment for it. Endurance and mindfulness are named as conditions rather than as causes. The help remains God's to extend. That holds together two things easily separated. One is the assurance that support exists. The other is the seriousness of what a person actually does while waiting for it.

crossReferences.why: Asks the question this ayah answers, about whether the first reinforcement would suffice.
Describes the moment later in this surah when holding fast gave way, and what followed.
Ties a promised advantage in battle to the state of the people receiving it.

studies.applyIt: The two conditions here are endurance and care. Both are unglamorous, and both are practised in advance rather than summoned in the moment. Pick one situation you know is coming and decide now, in writing if it helps, what holding your position will actually look like when it arrives.
studies.explainEasier: If you hold your ground and stay careful, they may still rush at you. Your Lord will then send even more help. Five thousand angels with clear marks on them will come down to your side.

studies.title: Only Good News For You
studies.meaning: The purpose of the reinforcement is stated plainly, and it is not military. God made it good news for you, and so that your hearts would settle. Then the point is made without hedging: help comes only from God. Classical commentators read this as correcting a natural misunderstanding, since a promise of thousands of angels invites the thought that the numbers are doing the work. The ayah says the numbers were for the hearts, and the outcome was never a matter of counting.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the passage about angelic reinforcement inside the account of the battle. Classical commentaries treat this ayah as the key to the two before it. It states what the promise was actually for. The surah's larger argument about the day is being set up here. The community's confidence had to be placed somewhere other than in a visible advantage.

keyTerms.note: From the root behind announcing glad tidings and the visible change in a face at good news. It names the message rather than the thing announced, which is precisely the distinction the ayah draws.
From a root describing ground that is level and still, and a heart at rest. It pictures reassurance as settling rather than as excitement, a quieter image than the English usually suggests.
From the root for coming to someone's aid, the same one used of the disciples earlier in this surah. It names assistance given, so victory is described as something received rather than achieved.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Morale was treated as a real thing in Arabian warfare. Commanders spread reports of allies coming, of fresh troops on the road, of an enemy's losses. A force that believed itself backed fought differently. Everyone knew that what men believed about their numbers mattered as much as the numbers.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying victory comes only from God appears twice in the Quran, here and in Surah 8. Both times it sits inside an account of a battle.
