They read it where it stands, as the natural close of a prayer that begins with reflection on creation and ends at the Day of Resurrection.

keyTerms.note: Not merely a promise but an arranged meeting, a place and a time agreed between two parties. The word turns the Day of Resurrection into an appointment that will be kept rather than an outcome that may arrive.

The same root used two verses earlier of those put into the Fire. Repeating it turns that earlier statement into a request, so the prayer asks not to fall on the wrong side of a sentence it just spoke.
The plural, not the singular. What is claimed is not a promise made to this community alone but the whole promise carried by every messenger, which is why the request can be made with confidence.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An appointment in Arabia was a serious thing, because keeping one was expensive. Meeting someone at a named well on a named day meant crossing desert on the strength of a word, with no way to confirm anything on the journey. A man who failed to appear was remembered for it for years. The words of this verse come from that world of arranged meetings honoured at cost.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a fixed appointment occurs four times in the Quran, twice in this surah and twice elsewhere. Three of the four are statements made about God in the third person. This one is the only place where the sentence is turned around and spoken straight to God, inside a prayer: You do not break the appointment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The request rests on what God is like, not on the record of the person asking. That is a particular kind of confidence. It also does something unusual with promises. Treating a promise from God as an appointment means two parties who both have to turn up. So the worry in the prayer is not whether God will keep the meeting. It is whether the speakers will be known when they get there.

crossReferences.why: Closes the first prayer of this surah with the same guarantee, stated about God rather than to Him.
Uses the same guarantee inside a passage about signs demanded and not supplied.
Asks for a promised thing in the same way, here in a prayer made by the angels.

studies.applyIt: There is something you have been half-asking God for without saying it out loud, because it feels presumptuous. Say it tonight in plain words, then add the reason this verse gives: not that you deserve it, but that He keeps appointments. Notice whether adding that reason changes how the asking feels in your mouth.
studies.explainEasier: Our Lord, give us what you promised us through your messengers. Do not shame us on the Day when everyone rises. We are asking because you always keep your word. You have never once broken a promise.

studies.title: You Are Of One Another
studies.meaning: The prayer is answered straight away, and the answer begins with a rule before it reaches any group. No worker's work is lost, and the verse names both kinds of worker on purpose: male or female. A short clause says why the two cannot be held apart in the accounting. Each is from the other. Only then does the answer turn to a set of people who left home, were driven out, were hurt, and fought. It promises them a covering over of their wrongs.
studies.historicalContext: This came down in Medina. The early sources report that a woman among the believers, Umm Salama, asked a question. The Quran had spoken of emigration and reward in the masculine, and yet women had emigrated and suffered too. This verse came in reply, and several early collections carry the report. The hardships listed here, being driven out, being hurt and fighting, describe what the Medinan community had by then lived through.

keyTerms.note: A form of the verb to answer that implies acting on a request rather than merely replying to it. The prayer of the four verses before it is met with a response that begins before any of it is restated.
The agent noun from the verb used throughout the Quran for deeds. Choosing the worker over the work makes the promise about persons: nobody who works goes unrecorded, whatever the work was.
From a root meaning to cover or conceal; the Quran uses the same root at 57:20 of sowers who bury seed under soil. Forgiveness is pictured as a covering rather than a denial that anything happened.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Emigration was not a journey but a taking apart. A household leaving Mecca sold nothing, since there was neither time nor a buyer. They walked out and left the house, the share in a well, the stored dates and the family graves. Women travelled in the same conditions as men, and some travelled alone. Some were held back by relatives who would not let them go.
studies.didYouKnow: The verse closes its list of hardships with two verbs built from a single root, one active and one passive: they fought, and they were killed. The classical reciters record more than one order for that pair, and early scholars discuss what each order implies. Nothing else in the list is doubled that way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: God does not do His accounting along the lines human societies use to rank people. The clause about being from one another is given as the reason, and it is a statement about where people come from rather than about what they are owed. The verse also does something careful with suffering. It does not explain it and does not call it good. It records it as work, and promises the work will not be lost.

crossReferences.why: States the same equality of reward for men and women, and adds a promise about this life.
Repeats the pairing in a legal setting, so the point is made twice in different registers.
Expands the pairing into a list of qualities named separately for men and for women.

studies.applyIt: Think of the work nobody sees you do: the early morning, the repeated cleaning, the phone call to a difficult relative. Name one piece of it today and let this verse's own word stand for it. Not a small thing that goes unnoticed. Work, of the kind this passage says is never wasted.
studies.explainEasier: God answered them: I will not waste the work of anyone who works, man or woman. You come from each other. Those who left their homes, were hurt and fought will have their sins covered and gardens to live in.

studies.title: The Comfort That Runs Out
studies.meaning: This is an instruction about attention rather than about belief. What it warns against is being taken in by movement: the visible activity of people doing well, travelling for trade, coming and going with obvious success. The passage does not deny the prosperity. It measures it as brief, and says what follows it. Then it sets the other side against that at much greater length, with verbs of staying. Early scholars gloss the word for their comings and goings as trade between markets.
studies.historicalContext: This falls near the close of the surah, in Medina. The Meccan opposition ran the caravan trade, and its wealth was on open display, while the Muslim community in Medina was poor. Early scholars report that some believers looked at that contrast and were unsettled by it. These verses answer the comparison rather than any argument. That is why they speak about being impressed rather than about being convinced.

keyTerms.note: From the verb to turn something over. Early scholars gloss it as travelling for trade, coming and going between markets, so what is described is visible commercial success rather than political power.
The same word names the baggage a traveller carries and the pleasure a thing gives. Both senses assume a journey: it is what you use on the way, not what you arrive holding.
What a host sets before a guest on arrival, before the real hospitality begins. Applied to the Gardens it makes them the reception rather than the whole of what is finally given.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The Meccan caravan year had a rhythm everyone in the Hijaz could watch. South towards Yemen in winter, north towards Syria in summer, hundreds of camels moving under armed guard. Wealth arrived in loads you could see, on animals you could count. For a poor household in Medina watching that traffic pass, the question of who was right could feel settled by what came down the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The two-word sentence calling it a brief enjoyment appears again, word for word, at 16:117, and there too a mention of punishment follows straight away. Elsewhere the Quran makes the same measurement at much greater length. Here it takes two words, set between a warning and a promise that both run far longer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Envy is treated here as a problem of seeing rather than a moral failing. The passage corrects it by adding what was missing, which is how long the thing lasts. It does not say the wealth is unreal or unearned. What it denies is that a snapshot amounts to a verdict. That leaves you room to admit somebody else's success honestly and still not want to trade places with them.

crossReferences.why: Uses almost the same sentence about not being deceived by their movement through the land.
Names the preference this passage corrects and gives two reasons, better and more lasting.
Applies the same word for brief enjoyment to everything given, not only to what opponents hold.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person whose life you have compared yourself to this month, probably on a screen. Instead of arguing yourself out of the feeling, add the missing information: what you actually know about their days, and what you do not. Envy usually runs on a very short clip. Lengthen it and most of its force goes.
studies.explainEasier: Do not be impressed by people who reject God moving about the land and doing well. It does not last long, and then their home is Hell. People who are careful of God get gardens with rivers, for good.

studies.title: Those Who Will Not Sell
studies.meaning: Near the end of a surah that has argued hard, a qualification arrives. After all that criticism, the passage says plainly that among the same communities are people who believe. They believe in this revelation and in what came to them, and they are lowered before God. The mark it gives is exact and negative: they do not sell the signs of God for a small price. Their reward is held with their Lord, out of reach of the argument that has been running.
studies.historicalContext: This is the second to last verse of the surah, from Medina. Early scholars most often connect it to the death of a ruler abroad who had sheltered Muslim emigrants years earlier and had come to believe, when news of it reached Medina and prayers were said. Other reports read the verse generally, of anyone from the earlier communities who accepted the message. Both readings are kept side by side.

keyTerms.note: The word describes a body as much as an attitude: eyes down, voice quiet, movement stilled. The Quran uses the same word at 41:39 of land that has gone flat and silent before rain arrives.
The word for what is paid, not for what is bought. The picture of selling revelation for a price runs through this surah, and here it finally shows up as something refused rather than taken.
A term from bookkeeping. Calling God swift at it says the tally is not a slow procedure, which matters at the close of a surah that has been counting things carefully for two hundred verses.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina was not a sealed city. Traders, travellers and refugees moved between it and Syria, Yemen and the far side of the Red Sea, and news about people travelled with them. A group of early Muslims had spent years abroad, under the protection of a foreign court. Communities were not the closed blocks later readers imagine. One family could hold several loyalties at once.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase about selling the signs of God for a small price occurs twice within a dozen verses in this surah. At 3:187 it is an accusation, and here at 3:199 it is praise. The same measure is applied to two groups drawn from the same communities, and it returns opposite results.
studies.theologicalSignificance: This verse stops a long argument from hardening into a verdict on a whole people. It takes nothing back from what was said earlier. It simply moves from communities to persons, and offers a test that a given person either meets or does not. It also treats reward as held with God, not handed out by any community. That takes the question of who counts as an insider out of human hands.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same qualification earlier in this surah, in almost the same terms and at greater length.
Describes the recognition itself, which this verse reports only as a finished fact.
Names people who believed on hearing it because of what they were already holding.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group you hold a settled opinion about, then name one actual person inside it whom you know. Notice how fast the general judgement stops applying. This verse does exactly that at the end of a long argument. You can do it in one sentence, before you next repeat something about a group.
studies.explainEasier: Not everyone who was given scripture before turned away. Some of them believe in God, in what came to you, and in what came to them. They are humble, and they will not sell the words of God cheaply.

studies.title: Endure, Outlast, Hold The Line
studies.meaning: Four commands come one after another, and each one asks more than the last. Be patient in your own difficulty. Then outlast others in it, which is what the reciprocal form of the verb means. The third comes from a root for tethering horses at a frontier, and is read as holding your position, staying bound to a post. Awareness of God follows those three. And the outcome is left as a hope rather than a guarantee, which early scholars point out about the closing word.
studies.historicalContext: The surah came down in Medina, and this is its final verse. It has spent much of its length on a defeat, on grief, and on argument with neighbours who rejected the message. Nothing more of the story is left to tell, so it ends with instructions instead. Early scholars report no particular occasion, and read this closing address as gathering up everything the surah has just worked through.

keyTerms.note: The root carries restraint and confinement, used of penning an animal or holding a person in place. Patience here is closer to staying put under pressure than to accepting something calmly.
A reciprocal form of the same verb, implying patience set against somebody else's, as in a contest of endurance. Early scholars read it as outlasting an opponent or as sustaining one another.
From the root for tying, and for the tether that binds a horse. Classical readings range from guarding a frontier to keeping yourself bound to prayer after prayer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Horses were rare and expensive in Arabia. Few people kept them, and they were prized above camels for speed. A man who tethered one at the edge of a settlement was committing a serious asset to waiting. He was feeding an animal that ate more than it earned, on the chance of a raid that might never come. The word chosen for the third command carries that picture of costly readiness.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of the four commands in this verse come from a single root, put into two different forms one after the other. Arabic can do that without sounding repetitive, because the second form turns the action outward towards somebody else. English needs two unrelated words to carry the shift.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Endurance is given three shapes rather than one, and they move outward: alone, then against a rival, then at a post held for others. That refuses the idea of patience as private resignation. The closing verb is left open, so even after all four commands the result is stated as something hoped for. Nothing in the sentence lets obedience turn into a claim on God.

crossReferences.why: Pairs patience with prayer as the two things to seek help through, and promises the company of God.
Ends its own short list with mutual counsel in patience, making endurance something exchanged.
Uses the same root for tethered horses, in the language of preparation and readiness.

studies.applyIt: Choose one thing you have been quitting again and again, and set a smaller version of it that you will keep for seven days. Not a better version, a smaller one. This verse puts holding position alongside enduring. Holding position means being there tomorrow, which is a different skill from trying hard today.
studies.explainEasier: Be patient when things are hard. Keep going longer than the people who are testing you. Stay at your post. Keep God in mind, and you may do well.
